x-ray: Before Wilhelm Röntgen, X-rays were noticed as an unidentified radiation coming from discharge tubes, by experimenters investigating cathode rays, the energetic electron beams first observed in 1869. Effects attributable to them appeared in many of the early Crookes tubes, invented around 1875. In these tubes a high direct-current voltage accelerated electrons so that they created X-rays when they struck the anode or the glass wall.

On 8 November 1895 Röntgen, a professor of physics, discovered X-rays while experimenting with Lenard tubes and Crookes tubes. On 28 December 1895 he submitted a preliminary communication, On a new kind of ray, to the journal of Würzburg's Physical-Medical Society, the first paper on X-rays. He called the radiation X to indicate an unknown type, and some early texts, taking the X for the Greek capital chi, speak of Chi-rays.

X-rays are electromagnetic radiation with wavelengths from about 10 nanometres to 10 picometres. Photons above about 5 to 10 keV are called hard X-rays and those of lower energy soft X-rays. There is no consensus on the boundary with gamma rays. One practice distinguishes them by source, X-rays coming from electron deexcitation and gamma rays from the decay of atomic nuclei, and another by wavelength.

X-rays are produced whenever charged particles of sufficient energy strike a material. The usual source is an X-ray tube, in which a high voltage accelerates electrons from a hot cathode into a metal target, the anode. In medical tubes the target is usually tungsten or an alloy of tungsten and rhenium. Bones show clearly on a radiograph because their calcium absorbs X-rays efficiently. Detectors were originally photographic plates and later film, and are now mostly digital.

Röntgen saw at once that X-rays could be used in medicine, and on 1 January 1896 he sent a letter to physicians he knew around Europe. The Scottish electrical engineer Alan Archibald Campbell-Swinton was the first after him to make an X-ray photograph, of a hand. By February there were 46 experimenters in North America alone. John Hall-Edwards made the first use under clinical conditions in Birmingham on 11 January 1896, radiographing a needle stuck in an associate's hand, and on 14 February 1896 he was the first to use X-rays in a surgical operation.

The hazards soon appeared, in stories of burns and hair loss. In February 1896 Professor John Daniel and William Lofland Dudley of Vanderbilt University reported hair loss after Dudley was X-rayed with an exposure of one hour. X-rays are ionising radiation and can cause DNA damage, burns, radiation sickness and cancer, yet the same property is used in radiotherapy to kill malignant cells. First-generation cold-cathode tubes of the Crookes type remained in use until about 1920.
xaltocan: Xaltocan lay at the centre of Lake Xaltocan, part of a system of shallow interconnected lakes that included Lake Texcoco; the site is now within the village of San Miguel Jaltocan in Nextlalpan, State of Mexico. Its name in Nahuatl may mean either sandy ground of spiders or where it is planted on the sand. The island was easy to fortify, and its people used the lake to build chinampas, raised fields on which they grew corn, beans, squash and other foods and produced a surplus.

The town's founding is told in the mytho-historical Historia Tolteca-Chichimeca and the Anales de Cuauhtitlan. According to the Anales the Xaltocameca, the people of Xaltocan, were among the Chichimec groups that left Aztlán under a leader named Quauhtliztac, White Eagle, and another account names their first leader Iztacquauhtli, a name of the same meaning. A lunar goddess, perhaps Zäna, was the town's leading deity, and Xaltocan is thought to have taken tribute from neighbouring city-states.

In the 13th century Xaltocan fought a long war with the Nahua city-state of Cuauhtitlan. Xaltocan was at first the stronger, but the ruler of Cuauhtitlan, Xaltemoctzin, allied himself with Tezozomoc of Azcapotzalco and the Mexica of Tenochtitlan, and the allies conquered the town. Its Otomí people fled north to Metztitlan and to Tlaxcala, while others were allowed to settle on lands of Texcoco at the place afterwards called Otumba, Place of the Otomies.

Over the following century Nahua peoples resettled the island. After the Aztec Triple Alliance defeated the Tepanecs of Azcapotzalco, Xaltocan became a subject town paying tribute to Tenochtitlan, mainly in woven blankets. The resettlement broke down the institutions that had kept its farming going, and the chinampas were eventually abandoned. In 1521, during the Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire, the army of Hernán Cortés razed the town and burned it to the ground.
xanthippus-father-of-pericles: Little is known of the early life of Xanthippus, a wealthy Athenian aristocrat and the son of Ariphron. His name means Yellow Horse. By 496 BCE he had married Agariste, niece of Cleisthenes, which tied him to the Alcmaeonid clan, whose interests he often represented, and their son Pericles was born around 495 BCE. He probably fought at the Battle of Marathon in 490 BCE.

In 489 BCE he appears in the record as the prosecutor of Miltiades the Younger, whom the Athenians suspected of treason after a failed attack on Paros. Xanthippus asked for the death penalty. Miltiades was fined a sum too large to pay and imprisoned as a debtor, and he died there of his wounds. Aristotle wrote that Xanthippus was at the head of the people while Miltiades represented the upper classes.

Xanthippus was ostracised in 484 BCE, probably as a result of his rivalry with Themistocles, with whom Aristides was also at odds. Of the 56 surviving ostraka naming him, one accuses him of disrespecting the prytaneion and another calls him a curse of the leaders. When the Persians invaded in 480 BCE, Athens recalled him and Aristides. He witnessed the Battle of Salamis, and in 479 BCE he was elected eponymous archon and succeeded Themistocles as commander of the Athenian fleet. At the Battle of Mycale, where about 250 Greek triremes pursued the Persians to the foot of Mount Mycale, he led the Athenian contingent on the left flank, which reached the enemy first.

Afterwards he led the Athenians, with Ionians and Aeolians, in the siege of Sestos in the Thracian Chersonese, which controlled the shipping on the Hellespont, on which Athens depended for imported grain. The siege lasted into the autumn and ended in winter, when food ran out. Herodotus says the Athenians stoned the son of the Persian governor Artayctes in front of him and then crucified Artayctes. Herodotus ends his account of the Persian Wars there, and some scholars suggest he wished to close on a note that flattered Pericles, one of his patrons.

Xanthippus died some years after returning to Athens, possibly in the mid-470s BCE, and was dead by 473/2 BCE, when Pericles served as choregos for Aeschylus. Pausanias records on the Athenian Acropolis a statue of him, who fought against the Persians at the naval battle of Mycale.
xanthos: Xanthos, called Arna in Lycian, stood on a hill on the left bank of the Xanthos river near the present village of Kınık in Antalya Province. Its acropolis dates from the 8th century BCE, and Strabo called it the largest city in Lycia. The sanctuary of Leto at Letoon, 4 kilometres to the south, dates from the late 6th century BCE and was linked to the city by a sacred road. The city was a centre of culture and commerce for the Lycians and later for the Persians, Greeks and Romans who conquered the region.

Herodotus and Appian describe the conquest of Xanthos by the Median general Harpagus for the Persian Empire. According to Herodotus, the Persians beat a small Lycian army north of the city about 540 BCE, and the Lycians retreated inside and were besieged. They destroyed their acropolis and killed their wives, children and slaves before a suicidal attack. Under Persian rule a local leadership was installed, coins were minted by 520 BCE and by 516 BCE the city appeared in the tribute list of Darius I.

Representatives of the cities of the Lycian League submitted to Alexander the Great at Xanthos. Arrian describes a peaceful surrender, while Appian says the city was sacked. Later Ptolemy I Soter took it from Antigonus I Monophthalmus. In 42 BCE Brutus besieged and destroyed Xanthos after the Lycian League refused to contribute funds, and only 150 men survived. Plutarch says the people set fire to their own city in a mass suicide. It was rebuilt under Mark Antony, and in the later Roman and Byzantine periods it gained luxury houses and several churches. Earthquakes in the sixth century damaged buildings, and the city was later destroyed and deserted.

The number and quality of its surviving tombs are the site's notable feature. The Nereid Monument inspired the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus in Caria. The Nereid Monument, the Tomb of Payava and the original sculptures of the Harpy Tomb are in the British Museum, while the Harpy Tomb stands in its original place with replica reliefs. Excavations have produced inscriptions in Lycian and Greek, including bilingual texts that help in understanding Lycian, and the trilingual Xanthian Obelisk records the older language called Milyan. Xanthos and Letoon were declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1988.
xavante: The Xavante, also called Shavante, Chavante, Akuen, Akwe, Awen or Akwen, number about 30,000 people in eastern Mato Grosso and speak the Xavante language of the Jê family. A genetic study of 2015 found that the Xavante, like the Paiter-Surui and Karitiana, have ancestry partly related to Indigenous peoples of the Andaman Islands, New Guinea and Australia. Scientists speculate that this goes back to an earlier East Asian population, called Population Y, from which both lines diverged 15,000 to 30,000 years ago.

The Xavante were enslaved in the 18th century and afterwards tried to avoid contact. A period of coexistence with Brazilian settler society in Goiás in the 19th century ended with their withdrawal to Mato Grosso between 1830 and 1860. Outsiders spoke of their rediscovery in the 1930s, and from 1946 to 1957 they were brought under Getúlio Vargas's National Integration Program, though they still suffered massacres and disease. This history left a lasting distrust of outsiders, whom the Xavante call waradzu.

The Xavante leader Mário Juruna became the first Indigenous Brazilian to sit as a federal representative. In 1996 the Brazilian band Sepultura stayed and recorded with the Xavante for its album Roots, and some Xavante travelled to São Paulo in 1998 to join the band's Barulho Contra Fome (Noise Against Hunger) concert.

Xavante society is divided into two clans, the Âwawẽ and the Po'reza'õno, and marriage within one's own clan is not allowed. The two clans meet in traditional log races, in which teams carry palm trunks weighing as much as 80 kg to a set point. Young men pass through elaborate initiation rites: at about fourteen small wooden sticks are inserted in their earlobes, and the ornaments are enlarged over the rest of their lives.
xavier-coppolani: Xavier Coppolani was born on 2 February 1866 at Marignana in Corsica. His father, Dominique, was counted among the colons, the French settlers of French Algeria. In Algeria Coppolani grew up among local Muslims and learnt Algerian Arabic, and he became intrigued by Islamic practice and studied Sufism.

In 1899 he was transferred to French Sudan to lead the expansion of colonial rule north of the Senegal River, where Moorish tribes held firm against the French. The mission was presented as an inquiry, but its aim was the subjugation of the local people. Using local tribal rivalries, in 1901 he drew up a plan for moving into the territory that combined military and political methods.

He made alliances with two leading marabouts of the Qadiriyya Sufi brotherhoods, Shaykh Sidya Baba and Shaykh Saad Bouh, promising them a dominant role in the colonial administration and protection for their Zawiya tribes against the attacks of Hassane warriors. In return they used their religious influence to persuade the emirs to accept French rule. Backed by military pressure, the plan worked, and the emirates of Tagant, Trarza and Brakna accepted French rule in 1903-04.

The northern emirate of Adrar resisted, backed by a third Qadiriyya marabout, Shaykh Ma al-'Aynayn, who was in turn supported by the Sultan of Morocco. Coppolani was preparing to march on Adrar when he was killed on 12 May 1905 by a member of the shaykh's Gudfiyya brotherhood. General Gouraud defeated Adrar and incorporated it by force into Mauritania in 1912, but tribal revolts and raids went on until 1934. Coppolani's work was instrumental in the colonial occupation and creation of modern Mauritania.
xenophanes: The ancient biographer Diogenes Laertius reports that Xenophanes was born in Colophon, a city of Ionia in present-day Turkey, and says he flourished in the 60th Olympiad (540–537 BCE). Modern scholars generally place his birth around 570–560 BCE. His surviving work refers to Thales, Epimenides and Pythagoras, and he is himself mentioned by Heraclitus and Epicharmus.

By his own account he was an itinerant poet who left his native land at the age of 25 and lived 67 years in other Greek lands, dying at or after the age of 92. Ancient testimony says he buried his sons, but little else about him or his family can be reliably established. His physical theories were probably influenced by the Milesians; his view that the rainbow is clouds may be read as a response to Anaximenes, who held that it is light reflected off clouds.

Xenophanes wrote a variety of poems, and his views are known only from fragments quoted by later writers. Diogenes Laertius says he wrote a poem of about 2,000 lines on the foundation of Colophon and Elea, and later testimony suggests his satires, called Silloi, filled at least five books. The title On Nature was probably given by librarians of the ancient world, and his remarks on natural philosophy were likely made incidentally in his satires. He composed elegiac couplets criticising traditional values of wealth, excess and athletic victory, and held that cultivating wisdom mattered more.

He criticised Homer and Hesiod for representing the gods as foolish or morally weak, and held that God is one, supreme among gods and men, and unlike mortals in body or mind. He sought natural explanations for clouds, rainbows and St. Elmo's fire. From fossils of sea creatures found above land he concluded that water had once covered the earth. He distinguished knowledge from belief, holding that an objective truth exists but that mortals cannot know it, and the sceptic Sextus Empiricus quotes his verses on the point.

Later ancient writers associated him with Elea, as founder of the Eleatic school and teacher of Parmenides and Zeno of Elea. Modern scholars generally find little justification for this, and note that no ancient writer expressly says he ever was at Elea. Timon of Phlius praised him as nearly a perfect sceptic, and the ancient tradition saw him as the first in a line leading to Pyrrhonism. He has been called the founder of epistemology, the first sceptic, an empiricist and a reformer of religion, while Karl Popper read him as a precursor of critical rationalism. Aristotle's Metaphysics summarised his view as the All is God.
xenophon: Xenophon was born in the Athenian deme of Erchia, the son of Gryllus, who belonged to an aristocratic family. The Peloponnesian War was fought through his childhood and youth. Like many wealthy young men of the time he associated with Socrates, and he probably served in the Athenian cavalry. He seems to have stayed in Athens under the Thirty Tyrants and to have fought the democratic insurgents in the civil war of 404 to 403 BCE. Xenophon was invited by Proxenus of Beotia to join the army that Cyrus the Younger was raising against the Persian satrap Tissaphernes.

Cyrus gathered a large army of Persians and Greeks, and the Greeks did not know at first that it was meant against King Artaxerxes II. After Cyrus was killed at the Battle of Cunaxa, the Spartan general Clearchus and four other generals were seized and executed on the invitation of Tissaphernes. The mercenaries, known as the Ten Thousand, then elected new leaders, among them Xenophon.

In the Anabasis he describes the retreat. The Greeks were harassed by Persian missile cavalry, fought the Carduchians in the mountains, forced a crossing of the Centrites River and marched through Armenia in winter without suitable clothing. They reached Trapezus on the Black Sea coast and fought the Colchians before making their way west. The military historian Theodore Ayrault Dodge called Xenophon the father of the system of retreat.

Afterwards Xenophon served with Spartan commanders in Anatolia and joined the campaign of King Agesilaus. Athens banished him for fighting on the Spartan side at the Battle of Coronea in 394 BCE. He received an estate at Scillus, where he lived for twenty-three years until the Elians confiscated it after Sparta's defeat at Leuctra in 371 BCE. According to Diogenes Laertius he then moved to Corinth.

Xenophon's whole body of work survives. It includes the Hellenica, which continues Thucydides' account of the Peloponnesian War to 362 BCE and is partial to Sparta, the Cyropaedia, the biography Agesilaus, the Constitution of the Lacedaemonians, and short treatises on horsemanship, hunting with dogs and the finances of Athens. His Socratic works are the Memorabilia, Apology, Symposium and Oeconomicus; apart from Plato's, they are the only surviving Socratic dialogues.

The Cyropaedia gives a fictional Cyrus the Great the qualities of an ideal ruler, and it differs from Herodotus on several points of his career. Some scholars read it as a warning that empires hold together only through a ruler of exceptional ability, and as a criticism of Athenian and Spartan ambitions for empire.
xerxes-i: Xerxes was born around 518 BCE, the son of Darius I and of Atossa, a daughter of Cyrus the Great. Greek sources describe the upbringing of Persian princes: raised by eunuchs, taught to ride and hunt from the age of seven, and given four aristocratic teachers from fourteen. It is unknown whether he learned to read or write. From 498 BCE he lived in the royal palace at Babylon.

When Darius prepared to go to Egypt in 487–486 BCE, Persian law required him to name a successor, and he chose Xerxes, his eldest son by Atossa, over Artobazan, who was born before Darius became king. Xerxes was crowned between October and December 486 BCE, at about thirty-two, and no one at court or among the subject nations is recorded as challenging him.

Xerxes put down a revolt in Egypt in January 484 BCE and made his full brother Achaemenes satrap there. Babylon rebelled at least twice: under Bel-shimanni in 484 BCE, a revolt that lasted about two weeks, and under Shamash-eriba from 482 BCE, defeated in March 481 BCE after a long siege. Afterwards Xerxes dropped the title King of Babylon and divided the large Babylonian satrapy into smaller units. Classical authors claim he wrecked the temples and removed the statue of Marduk, which the modern historian Amélie Kuhrt considers unlikely.

From 483 BCE he prepared the invasion of Greece, with a canal cut through the Athos peninsula and two pontoon bridges over the Hellespont. In 480 BCE he marched from Sardis. After Thermopylae and Artemisium he took and burned Athens, then lost the sea battle at Salamis. He withdrew with most of his army, leaving Mardonius, who was defeated at Plataea the next year. Back in Persia he finished works begun by Darius at Persepolis, including the Gate of All Nations and the Apadana, and built a palace at Susa.

In August 465 BCE Artabanus, commander of the royal guard, killed Xerxes with the help of the eunuch Aspamitres. Ctesias says Artabanus then blamed the crown prince Darius, while Aristotle says he killed Darius first. Xerxes's son Artaxerxes I took the throne. Xerxes held to Ahura Mazda as supreme deity, though scholars do not agree whether he was influenced by Zoroastrianism.

Greek and Roman sources present him largely in a negative light. Aeschylus's play The Persians (472 BCE) shows a hubristic ruler, and Herodotus gives a fuller portrait that Richard Stoneman reads as nuanced and tragic, while Pierre Briant calls it biased. He is identified with Ahasuerus in the Book of Esther, and is the hero of Handel's opera Serse (1738).
xhosa-people: The Xhosa are descendants of Nguni clans who settled in the southeastern part of Southern Africa. These farming agropastoralists brought cattle and goats, absorbed weaker San groups and formed chiefdoms and kingdoms, mainly in what is now the Eastern Cape. Archaeological evidence suggests that Xhosa-speaking people have lived in the area since at least the 7th century. According to oral tradition the Xhosa Kingdom was founded before the 15th century by Tshawe, after whom the royal clan is named, who overthrew his brother Cirha with the help of the amaNgwevu clan of the amaMpondomise Kingdom. Khoekhoe groups such as the Inqua and the Giqwa were incorporated and became tributary to the amaTshawe.

After Europeans settled the Cape in 1652 the Khoisan were gradually pushed eastwards, and by the 1700s the Cape Colony's borders had moved far enough east to create a hostile population ready to resist in the Eastern Cape. This began the Cape frontier wars, some of the longest military resistance to colonialism. Large parts of the native population were confined to reserves in the easternmost Cape, though they also continued to serve as labour inside the colony. These reserves were later renamed homelands and were dismantled in 1994.

In the 19th century the Xhosa fought off and took in many peoples fleeing the Zulus during the mfecane. The Xhosa called those they accepted amaMfengu, meaning wanderers, among them the amaBhaca, amaHlubi and amaZizi. Xhosa unity and their ability to resist colonial encroachment were weakened by the famines and divisions that followed the cattle-killing movement that began in 1856. Historians now see it as a millennialist response, directly to a lung disease spreading among their cattle and indirectly to the strain of losing territory and autonomy.

Cattle are important and the basis of wealth, and the Xhosa settled on the slopes of the Amatola and Winterberg Mountains, where the Kei and Fish Rivers and rich soils suit farming and grazing. Traditional foods include beef, mutton, goat, sorghum, maize meal, amasi, a fermented milk, and umqombothi, a beer of fermented maize and sorghum. Marriage, umtshato, involves a sequence of customs including the discussion of the woman's clan name, isiduko, since people sharing a clan name may not marry, and lobola negotiations, which were traditionally settled in cattle and are now often paid in money. The speakers of isiXhosa, a Bantu tonal language written in the Latin alphabet, understand Zulu to some degree.
xia-shang-zhou-chronology-project: Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian could give a year-by-year chronology only back to the Gonghe Regency of 841 BCE; for earlier times it offered king lists and isolated events. In the 1920s Gu Jiegang and the Doubting Antiquity School argued that the traditional history had gathered layers of myth, and some doubted even the Shang. Oracle bones, identified as writing by Wang Yirong in 1899 and traced in 1928 to Yinxu near Anyang, then yielded a sequence of Shang kings close to Sima Qian's list.

In 1994 Song Jian, a state councillor for science, was impressed on a visit to Egypt by its chronologies reaching back to the 3rd millennium BCE and proposed a similar project for China. It was approved as part of the ninth five-year plan, directed by Li Xueqin of Tsinghua University, and involved around 200 experts.

The project combined archaeology, radiocarbon dating, textual study and astronomy. For the Western Zhou it used about 60 dated bronze inscriptions and took the double dawn at King Yih's accession as an annular solar eclipse of 899 BCE, a reading first proposed by the Korean scholar Pang Sunjoo. Radiocarbon dates from Fengxi and from late Yinxu and early Zhou capitals narrowed the conquest of the Shang to between 1050 and 1020 BCE, within which only 20 January 1046 BCE matched all the astronomical records. It assigned all four phases of the Erlitou culture to the Xia and placed the Shang's foundation at the walled city of Yanshi.

Critics noted that the radiocarbon ranges were cited at a 68 per cent confidence interval rather than the standard 95 per cent, that the link between site layers and the conquest is uncertain, and that a key text, the Li gui inscription, can be read to give 9 January 1044 BCE. David Nivison was among those who criticised the methods at the Association for Asian Studies in 2002, and others objected that it reduced archaeology to confirming traditional histories. The Harvard archaeologist Yun Kuen Lee judged that politics did not shape its detailed work.

Bronzes found after 2000, such as the Jue Gong gui and the Jun gui, give reign years that conflict with its Western Zhou dates. The final report, published in June 2022, acknowledged many such problems but kept the table of 2000 unchanged, and the project's dates have become the orthodox chronology of Chinese textbooks and reference works.
xian: Xi'an lies on the Guanzhong Plain in the south-central part of Shaanxi province, on a flood plain made by eight surrounding rivers and streams. It borders the northern foot of the Qin Mountains to the south and the banks of the Wei River to the north. Hua Shan, one of the five sacred Taoist mountains, is about 100 km to the east, and the Loess Plateau lies not far to the north. The climate is temperate, influenced by the East Asian monsoon, with hot, humid summers and cold, dry winters.

The Lantian Man, discovered in 1963 in Lantian County 50 km southeast of the city, dates to at least 500,000 years before the present. Banpo, a Neolithic village found in 1953 on the eastern outskirts, contains the remains of several well-organised settlements carbon dated to 5,600 to 6,700 years ago.

The area became a cultural and political centre of China in the 11th century BCE with the founding of the Zhou dynasty, whose capital stood in the twin settlements of Fengjing and Haojing, together called Fenghao, southwest of the modern city. King Ping of Zhou later moved the capital to Luoyang because of political unrest. After the Warring States period the Qin dynasty, which ruled from 221 to 206 BCE, unified China from its capital at Xianyang, just northwest of Xi'an. Qin Shi Huang ordered the building of the Terracotta Army and his mausoleum, east of the city, almost as soon as he took the throne.

Under the name Chang'an, the city held the position of capital under several of the most important dynasties, including the Western Han, Sui, Northern Zhou and Tang. The present name, 西安, Western Peace, was adopted in 1369 under the early Ming dynasty. Jesuit missionaries recorded it as Si-ngan or Si-ngan-fou, after its status as a prefectural seat. The Qing dynasty set up a walled Manchu banner quarter in the northeast, on the site of the former palace of the Ming Prince of Qin, and a Han banner quarter in the southeast.

Xi'an is the capital of Shaanxi province and the most populous city in Northwestern China. It is counted among China's Five Great Ancient Capitals. The Mausoleum of the First Qin Emperor with the Terracotta Army lies near it, and five component sites of the UNESCO-listed Silk Roads: the Routes Network of Chang'an-Tianshan Corridor are in the city. Chinese Standard Time is set by the National Time Service Center near Lintong.
xian-incident: The Chinese Communist Party and the Nationalists had been at war since 1927. After the Japanese invasion of Manchuria in 1931, Chiang Kai-shek ordered General Zhang Xueliang not to resist and adopted the policy of first internal pacification, then external resistance. In October 1935 the Communists reached northern Shaanxi at the end of the Long March, having lost over 90 percent of their numbers. They were hemmed in by the Northeastern Army under Zhang, 130,000 strong, and the Northwestern Army under Yang Hucheng, 40,000 strong, both based at Xi'an. Secret talks between the two parties in 1936 stalled, while the Communists forged a covert alliance with both armies.

Chiang flew to Xi'an on 4 December 1936 to prepare another assault on the Communists. On 9 December he threatened Zhang and Yang with removal and the reassignment of their forces to distant southern provinces. The historian Rana Mitter suggests that this may have confirmed Zhang's intention to act. On 12 December they seized Chiang and demanded an end to the civil war and an alliance with the Communists against Japan. Mao Zedong at first approved putting Chiang on trial.

Joseph Stalin, fearing a Japanese plot to weaken China, overruled the Communists and ordered a peaceful resolution. General He Yingqin nearly launched an assault on Xi'an before Soong Mei-ling and T. V. Soong prevailed in favour of negotiation. Zhou Enlai, Qin Bangxian and Ye Jianying joined the talks, and Zhou persuaded Yang's faction and the young officers who wanted to execute Chiang to negotiate his release. Chiang conceded to a ceasefire, and on 25 December Zhang released him and flew with him to Nanjing.

Chiang was greeted in Nanjing by cheering crowds of over 400,000 people and immediately had Zhang arrested; Zhang remained under house arrest until 1990. Yang was arrested in 1937 and executed in Chongqing shortly before the city fell to the Communists in 1949. The final pieces of the Second United Front were agreed in late September 1937, after the Second Sino-Japanese War had begun.

The incident is the subject of often partisan histories. To the Nationalists it was a lost opportunity to destroy the Communists. In the Communist account the party was the country's saviour, committed to resistance while Chiang obstinately put the civil war first. Zhou Enlai called Zhang Xueliang a hero of the nation, and Zhang said in the 1990s that he had no regrets.
xianbei: The Xianbei were probably not a single ethnic group but a multilingual confederation, made up mainly of Proto-Mongols and, to a smaller degree, Tungusic and Turkic peoples. They are said to descend from the Donghu, who split into the Wuhuan and the Xianbei when the Xiongnu defeated them at the end of the 3rd century BCE. In the 1st century BCE the Xianbei took part in the conflict between the Han dynasty and the Xiongnu, and they came to replace the Xiongnu on the Mongolian Plateau. In the mid-2nd century the chieftain Tanshihuai united the tribes, took the title Daren, or Elder, and divided his realm into three sections, each under an appointed chieftain.

By the Jian'an era (196-220) the Xianbei had divided into many groups. After the warlord Cao Cao destroyed the Wuhuan confederacy in 207, the fractured tribes began to pay tribute to the Chinese court. Around the turn of the 4th century, Xianbei and Wuhuan auxiliaries under Wang Jun fought in the War of the Eight Princes of the Western Jin dynasty and helped to capture Ye in 304 and Chang'an in 306, but also took part in the sackings. In the Sixteen Kingdoms period the Xianbei founded several short-lived states.

The Tuoba founded the Northern Wei after the collapse of the Former Qin. In 395 the Murong state of Later Yan was defeated at Canhe Slope, and within three years the Tuoba took most of present-day Shanxi and Hebei. In 493 Emperor Xiaowen moved the capital from Pingcheng to Luoyang, partly because Pingcheng had suffered drought and cattle plague in 487 and 50 to 60 per cent of its people had left. His policies suppressed Xianbei customs and promoted Han language, dress and rituals. A rebellion of six frontier garrisons in 524 led to the split of the Northern Wei into eastern and western regimes.

The Northern dynasties led or strongly influenced by the Xianbei merged with the general Chinese population by the Tang dynasty. Descendants of the Northern Wei royal family survived into the Tang, among them the chancellor Zhangsun Wuji and the poet Yuan Zhen, and the Sui and Tang governments and armies rested on institutions created by the Xianbei dynasties. The Xianbei language faded: the Book of Sui, completed in 636, records that many Xianbei of the Central Plains no longer understood it. Eighth-century Turkic inscriptions call China Tabgach, from Tuoba, and the Karakhanid rulers later used the title Tamghaj Khan.
xiang-army: The Taiping Rebellion began in Guangxi in December 1850, and in March 1853 the Taiping took Nanjing, which became their capital. In 1852 the Qing court had appointed Zeng Guofan commissioner of militia organisation for Central China. He expanded the existing village militia, the tuanlian, into a force of 17,000 men, with thirteen battalions of infantry and ten of navy, which took orders from Zeng alone. Its principle, that soldiers followed and belonged to their general, broke with older practice and is seen as a direct cause of the later warlord era.

Funded at first by diverting provincial toll revenues and later by levies on landholders and merchants, the army recovered Changsha, Wuchang and Hanyang. The court soon used it in place of its own troops, and in 1860 Zeng was sent to clear Anhui and made Viceroy of Liangjiang. That year the Xiang Army numbered almost 360,000 soldiers, 130,000 under Zeng himself. After the area around Nanjing was cleared from June 1863, the assault on the city began on 14 March 1864. On 19 July explosives packed into tunnels brought down a large part of the wall, and the city fell after three days of fighting.

The army then pillaged and burned Nanjing, killing 100,000 Taiping soldiers and civilians according to Zeng, and the fires burned until 26 July 1864. Zeng disbanded the 120,000 men under his command soon afterwards, though Zuo Zongtang kept his forces, which numbered about 120,000 in the 1870s. From 1864 to 1890 more than half of China's viceroys were Xiang Army leaders.

The basic unit was the ying, a battalion of 5 officers and 500 soldiers, or 688 men with administrators and carriers, divided into four companies and a bodyguard. Its arms were mortars, jingals, spears, swords and matchlocks, and by 1864 some squads carried foreign rifles. Senior commanders often chose their juniors from among relatives and friends. Zeng held that good pay sustained morale: a soldier received four taels of silver a month, against about 1.5 for a soldier of the Green Standard Army.
xiang-yu: Xiang Yu was born in 232 BCE, in the late Warring States period. Two accounts of his family exist. One makes him a member of the royal house of Chu, whose ancestors received Xiang County as a fief. The other makes him a descendant of a noble clan of Lu whose family had served in the Chu army for generations. His grandfather Xiang Yan, a general, was killed resisting a Qin invasion in 223 BCE, and his uncle Xiang Liang raised him. Watching Qin Shi Huang's procession pass on an inspection tour, he said, I can replace him.

In 209 BCE uprisings broke out across China. Xiang Yu and Xiang Liang killed Yin Tong, the Qin administrator of Kuaiji, and Xiang Liang gathered about 8,000 men, a force that grew to between 60,000 and 70,000. In 208 BCE they installed Mi Xin as King Huai II of Chu. In 207 BCE Xiang Yu killed the commander Song Yi and took command. At Julu he ordered his men to sink their boats and destroy all but three days of rations, and his force defeated a Qin army of 300,000 in nine engagements.

After Ziying, the last Qin emperor, surrendered to Liu Bang in winter 207 BCE, Xiang Yu planned to have him killed at a feast at Swan Goose Gate but spared him on the advice of his uncle Xiang Bo. In spring 206 BCE he divided the Qin lands into the Eighteen Kingdoms, took the title Hegemon-King of Western Chu with its capital at Pengcheng, and sent Liu Bang to Hanzhong as King of Han. The nominal ruler, now Emperor Yi of Chu, was exiled and killed by Ying Bu on Xiang Yu's order.

In 205 BCE Liu Bang took Pengcheng with allied armies, but Xiang Yu returned with 30,000 troops and defeated him there. By 203 BCE the tide had turned, and the Treaty of Hong Canal divided China between them. Liu Bang broke it, and in 202 BCE the forces of Liu Bang, Han Xin and Peng Yue trapped Xiang Yu at Gaixia. He broke out with about 800 horsemen, and by Dongcheng he had 28 men left, declaring that Heaven, not his own failings, had brought his fall. He died by suicide.

The historian Sima Qian judged him boastful, reliant on his own abilities and cruel, since he ordered the massacre of cities that had surrendered, and thought it ridiculous that he blamed Heaven. Modern historians compare his military skill to that of Hannibal. Mao Zedong named three reasons for his downfall, among them sparing Liu Bang at the feast and building his capital at Pengcheng.
xiangtangshan-caves: The caves, whose name means Mountain of the Echoing Halls, lie in the Fengfeng Mining District, about 20 km southwest of Handan and about 20 km northwest of the site of Ye, the Northern Qi capital. They were carved into dense limestone cliffs of the Taihang Mountains. There are 36 caves in three groups: a northern group on Mount Gu near the village of Hecun, a southern group on Mount Fu, and a site at Shuiyusi known as Little Xiangtangshan.

According to the monk Min Fen, the northern group was commissioned by Wen Xuan, the first Northern Qi emperor. Its largest cave, the northern cave or cave 7, has an elevated empty niche atop its central pillar that historical sources and scholars identify as the burial chamber of Gao Yang or of his father, Gao Huan. Recent research has reconstructed seven limestone caryatid panels, now scattered among collections, as the base of a memorial stupa once placed in this niche.

The southern group was begun in 565 by the monk Hui Yi of the Linghua temple and continued under the patronage of Gao Anahong, the king of Huai Ying and one of the highest officials of the dynasty. Without imperial patrons its caves are smaller than the northern ones, and work there probably ended about the time the Northern Zhou annexed the Northern Qi in 577.

Sculptures were removed and sold abroad as early as 1909. The dealer C.T. Loo, suspected of arranging their removal from China without permission, sold a number to the American collector Charles Freer. Pieces are now held by the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Freer Gallery, the Cleveland Museum of Art, the Victoria and Albert Museum, the Miho Museum and others, the Freer holding the Western Paradise relief panel from South Cave 2. The Center for the Art of East Asia at the University of Chicago used 3D scanning and archival photographs to match scattered sculptures to their caves, leading to the exhibition Echoes of the Past. The caves are a Major Historical and Cultural Site Protected at the National Level.
xiangyang: Xiangyang stands at a strategic site on the middle reaches of the Han River, a major tributary of the Yangtze, which runs through the centre of the city and divides it north from south. The modern city is an agglomeration of two formerly separate cities, Fancheng to the north of the river and Xiangyang, also called Xiangcheng, to the south. What remains of old Xiangyang contains one of the oldest still-intact city walls in China. The two cities were merged in 1950 as Xiangfan, and the name Xiangyang was restored in 2010.

Xiangyang County was first established at the site of modern Xiangcheng in the early Western Han dynasty, and the name was used continuously for more than 2,000 years. In the last years of the Eastern Han it became the capital of Jing Province, and the warlord Liu Biao governed from here. Under his rule it became a destination for northern elites fleeing the warfare of the Central Plain. In the Battle of Xiangyang in 191 the rival warlord Sun Jian, father of Sun Quan, the founder of Eastern Wu, was defeated and killed. The Battle of Fancheng, two decades later, was one of the most important of the late Han and Three Kingdoms period and cost Liu Bei Jingzhou.

In the early Jin dynasty Xiangyang lay on the frontier with Eastern Wu. Its commander Yang Hu was remembered for a policy of border peace that allowed cross-border commerce, and the city accumulated supplies for ten years, which played a key part in the Jin conquest of Wu. After the Treaty of Shaoxing it became a garrison city on the northern frontier of the Southern Song. During the Mongol conquest of the Song, Xiangyang and Fancheng together formed one of the main obstacles to Mongol expansion, resisting for six years before surrendering in the Siege of Xiangyang.

In 1796 Xiangyang was one of the centres of the White Lotus Rebellion against the Qing, where the rebel leader Wang Cong'er organised an army of 50,000 and joined the main rebel forces in Sichuan. The revolt lasted nearly ten years.

Xiangyang is a prefecture-level city in northwestern Hubei, and the railways to Chongqing, Hankou–Danjiangkou and Jiaozuo–Liuzhou meet at Fancheng. It is the home of the Dongfeng Motors company. The city's boundaries in their present form date from 1983, when Xiangyang Prefecture was incorporated into Xiangfan City.
xianyang: Xianyang lay among the capital's environs under the Western Zhou and was made the capital of the state of Qin in 350 BCE, during the Warring States period. It was named Xianyang, meaning fully yang, because it lay south of the Jiuzong Mountains and north of the Wei River, both sunlit orientations. Under Duke Xiao of Qin the minister Shang Yang designed the city and organised the move of the administration from the old capital Yueyang. It remained the capital for over 140 years.

In 221 BCE Qin Shi Huang eliminated the six other warring states and established the first centralised empire in Chinese history. Noble families were compelled to move to Xianyang, and the weapons of the realm were gathered there to be melted into twelve towering statues. He expanded the city beyond its walls, built replicas of the palaces of the conquered states along the Wei River and a network of 300 palaces connected by elevated roads, and in 212 BCE began the Epang Palace. His lavish mausoleum, with the Terracotta Army, stood near the capital. These undertakings drew huge amounts of manpower and resources from agriculture and, together with repression, led to the fall of the dynasty.

After the First Emperor died in 210 BCE revolts broke out. In December 207 BCE the last Qin emperor, Ziying, surrendered to the rebel Liu Bang, who entered peacefully. Liu Bang had to hand the city to the more ruthless Xiang Yu, who killed Ziying and burned Xianyang in 206 BCE, destroying the only surviving copies of several banned books in the royal library.

Under the Han the part of Xianyang south of the Wei River was absorbed into Chang'an and the north became Weicheng County. Liu Bang, as Emperor Gaozu of Han, chose a high plain at Xianyang for his mausoleum, and many successors followed. Five mausoleum towns were established there and prominent families resettled in them, so that Wuling, the Five Mausoleums, became a name for the empire's elite. In the Tang period Weicheng held the first relay station out of Chang'an on the road to the western frontiers, and Wang Wei's poem A Song at Weicheng became a classic of farewell poetry. The present Xianyang was established in 1371, early in the Ming dynasty.

Xianyang is a prefecture-level city of Shaanxi, part of the Greater Xi'an Metropolitan Area, and the Xi'an Xianyang International Airport stands in it. Archaeologists have excavated many Qin sites there since the late 1950s, including palaces, workshops and tombs. The city has one UNESCO World Heritage Site and many Han and Tang imperial mausoleums, and it is the home of the Ban family of historians, Ban Gu, Ban Chao and Ban Zhao.
xiao-baojuan: Born Xiao Mingxian in 483, he was the second son of Xiao Luan and of his wife Liu Huiduan. In 494 Xiao Luan, prime minister to the young Xiao Zhaoye, overthrew him, killed many sons of Emperor Wu and Emperor Gao and took the throne as Emperor Ming. Because his elder brother Xiao Baoyi was said to be severely disabled and unable to speak, Xiao Baojuan was made crown prince. He was said to dislike study and prefer games, and his father often urged him to act decisively. He succeeded in the autumn of 498.

Emperor Ming's will left the government to a group of officials, among them Xiao Yaoguang, Xu Xiaosi, Jiang Shi and Liu Xuan. When Jiang Shi discussed replacing him with his brother Xiao Baoxuan, the emperor had Jiang Shi and Jiang Si executed, and he put down Xiao Yaoguang's revolt in 499. Within months he had Xiao Tanzhi, Liu Xuan, Cao Hu, Xu Xiaosi and Shen Wenji killed. The general Chen Xianda rebelled and died in battle near the capital around the new year of 500, and Pei Zhaoye surrendered Shouyang to Northern Wei.

Sent to retake Shouyang, Cui Huijing turned against the emperor, won over Xiao Baoxuan and besieged the palace, but Xiao Yi defeated him. Xiao Baojuan favoured his consort Pan Yunu, whose father Pan Baoqing had people falsely accused and executed to seize their property, and he demanded luxury goods and built heavily. When he went out, guards first expelled people from the streets, and anyone who did not leave was executed. In the winter of 500 he forced Xiao Yi to commit suicide.

Xiao Yan rebelled from Xiangyang, and Xiao Yingzhou declared the emperor's brother Xiao Baorong emperor at Jiangling, so that Southern Qi had two emperors for several months. The generals Wang Zhenguo and Zhang Ji at first defended Jiankang well, but when they learned the emperor's associates doubted their loyalty they had him assassinated and sent his head to Xiao Yan. Consort Pan was executed, and Empress Chu and Crown Prince Song were reduced to commoners. By 502 Xiao Yan had ended Southern Qi and founded the Liang dynasty.
xiao-cha: Xiao Cha, courtesy name Lisun, was born in 519 as the third son of Xiao Tong, crown prince of the Liang dynasty's founder Emperor Wu, and his concubine Consort Gong. He was studious and devoted to Buddhist sutras, which pleased his devout grandfather. When Xiao Tong died in 531, Emperor Wu made his own son Xiao Gang crown prince instead of Xiao Tong's eldest son. To make amends he created Xiao Tong's sons princes, Xiao Cha becoming Prince of Yueyang, but Xiao Cha resented being passed over. Made governor of Yong Province in 546, he governed carefully to build a power base of his own.

After the general Hou Jing rebelled in 548, Xiao Cha's brother Xiao Yu, governor of Xiang Province, quarrelled with their uncle Xiao Yi, who besieged him at Changsha. Xiao Cha attacked Xiao Yi's headquarters at Jiangling, but heavy rain, the general Wang Sengbian and the defection of his own general Du Ze drove him back to Xiangyang. Fearing he would be next, he submitted to the Western Wei as a vassal and sent his wife and heir as hostages. The Western Wei general Yang Zhong defeated Xiao Yi's forces in 550, and Xiao Yu was executed. Xiao Cha declined Western Wei's offer to make him emperor that year but accepted the title Prince of Liang.

Xiao Yi declared himself emperor at Jiangling in 552 and treated the Western Wei with arrogance, and Xiao Cha encouraged the Western Wei paramount general Yuwen Tai to invade. Xiao Cha's forces joined the invading army under Yu Jin, Jiangling fell and Emperor Yuan surrendered. Xiao Cha took custody of him and insulted him, and around the new year 555 Emperor Yuan was put to death with Western Wei approval, together with his captured sons.

In exchange for Jiangling, Western Wei took the Xiangyang region and kept a garrison in the city; its troops carried most of Jiangling's people and the Liang treasures to Chang'an. Xiao Cha refused advice to attack the garrison, though he later regretted it. The Liang generals, among them Wang Lin, never recognised him. After 560 he briefly held more of Hunan with Northern Zhou help, but by 561 the Chen dynasty had taken it, leaving him only the Jiangling region. Depressed and ill with a lesion on his back, he died in spring 562 and was succeeded by his son Xiao Kui. He left 15 scrolls of literary works and 36 of commentary on Buddhist sutras.
xiao-cong: Xiao Cong, courtesy name Wenwen, was a son of Xiao Kui, Emperor Ming of Western Liang. He was first created Prince of Dongyang rather than crown prince, which suggests that he was the second son. In his youth he was considered knowledgeable and free-spirited. He was crown prince by 583, when his father sent him to congratulate the Western Liang's suzerain, Emperor Wen of Sui, on moving his capital to the newly built city of Daxing. He succeeded his father in 585.

In 585 he sent his general Qi Xin against the Chen dynasty's city of Gong'an, without success. The same year Emperor Wen summoned Xiao Cong's uncle Xiao Cen to Daxing and kept him there, restored the post of Commandant of Jiangling and posted troops in the Western Liang capital, reasserting his control of the state. One of Xiao Cong's generals, Xu Shiwu, secretly offered to submit to the Chen general Chen Huiji; Xiao Cong discovered the plot and executed him.

In 587 Xiao Cong set out for the Sui capital with a train of some 200 officials, while the people of Jiangling wept, believing he would not return. When the Sui general Cui Hongdu approached, Xiao Cong's uncle Xiao Yan and brother Xiao Huan suspected an attack, offered their surrender to Chen Huiji and led the people of Jiangling into Chen territory. Emperor Wen then abolished the Western Liang by edict and made Xiao Cong Duke of Ju.

After Emperor Wen's death in 604, his son Emperor Yang, whose wife Empress Xiao was Xiao Cong's younger sister, made him Duke of Liang and gave posts to several of his relatives. Xiao Cong held high office but rarely carried out its duties, explaining to the official Yang Yue in veiled terms that he did not wish to draw attention to himself. He also refused to yield to the great clans of the north, and so offended many northern nobles.

In 607 Emperor Yang killed Gao Jiong, Heruo Bi and Yuwen Bi for criticising his rewards to the Qimin Khan of the Tujue. Xiao Cong had been a close friend of Heruo Bi, and a popular song with the line "Xiao Xiao will rise again" deepened the emperor's suspicion. Xiao Cong was removed from office and died at home. His nephew Xiao Ju inherited his title, and in 617 the rebel Xiao Xian, who briefly restored Liang, honoured him as Emperor Jing.
xiao-daocheng: Xiao Daocheng's family traced its line to Xiao He, the Western Han chancellor, and had served as minor officials under the Jin and Liu Song. His father, Xiao Chengzhi, was a general of Emperor Wen of Song, made Baron of Jinxing for campaigns against Northern Wei. At 12 Xiao studied the Confucian classics at the imperial university headed by Lei Cizong, but by 15 he was in the army.

In the succession war of 466 he sided with Emperor Ming, fought the forces of Liu Zifang and defeated the army sent by Xue Andu, and was made Marquess of Xiyang and governor of Southern Yan Province, defending Huaiyin. In 471 the suspicious emperor sent him a sealed pot of wine; he drank only after the envoy, his friend Wu Xi, tasted it first.

When Liu Xiufan, Prince of Guiyang, rebelled in 474, Xiao proposed holding the forts outside Jiankang, and his officers Huang Hui and Zhang Jing'er killed the prince after pretending to surrender. Xiao then shared power with Yuan Can, Chu Yuan and Liu Bing as one of the four nobles. In 477 the 14-year-old Emperor Houfei, whose violence was feared, used Xiao's belly as a target for blunt arrows; afterwards Xiao had an attendant, Yang Yufu, kill the emperor in his sleep.

He set up Liu Zhun as Emperor Shun. Yuan Can and Liu Bing plotted against him, but Chu Yuan warned him, and his troops killed both at Shitou Cheng. The rising of Shen Youzhi of Jing Province stalled before Yingcheng in 478 and ended with Shen's suicide. In 479 Xiao was made Duke and then Prince of Qi and given the nine bestowments, and that summer he took the throne.

As Emperor Gao he called for frugality and an end to luxury, though how far his officials heeded him is unclear. Later in 479 the guards watching the former Emperor Shun killed him in a panic; Gao rewarded them and massacred the Liu Song imperial clan. A Northern Wei attack that winter, made in the name of the exiled Liu Chang, Prince of Danyang, ended after a failed siege of Shouyang, and Gao began building the first wall around Jiankang. He died on 11 April 482 and was succeeded by his son Xiao Ze as Emperor Wu.
xiao-he: Xiao He was born in Fengyi County, in present-day Feng County, Jiangsu, and served as a magistrate's secretary in the office of Pei County. He was well versed in law and had a wide circle of friends that included Liu Bang, Cao Shen, Fan Kuai, Xiahou Ying and Zhou Bo. When rebellions spread after the Dazexiang Uprising of 209 BCE, he and Cao Shen fled the magistrate of Pei, who meant to execute them, and joined Liu Bang. The story is told that when the townsfolk drew lots for a leader, Xiao He had written Liu Bang's name on every slip.

When Liu Bang's army entered the Qin capital Xianyang in 206 BCE, Xiao He went straight to the chancellor's office and saved its documents, which he valued above treasure for what they told of the empire. After Xiang Yu made Liu Bang King of Han and sent him to the remote Bashu region, Xiao He became chancellor of the Han kingdom. There he rode after Han Xin, who had deserted, for several days and nights, brought him back and persuaded Liu Bang to make him Grand Marshal.

While Liu Bang fought Xiang Yu in the east, Xiao He governed Guanzhong and Bashu, lowered the taxes of the poor and gave former Qin aristocratic land to peasants. After the victory at Gaixia in 202 BCE, when Liu Bang became Emperor Gaozu, Xiao He was made Marquis of Zan, with the rare right to enter court wearing his sword and shoes. He oversaw the building of the Weiyang Palace at the new capital, renamed Chang'an. In 196 BCE he helped Empress Lü Zhi lure Han Xin, accused of conspiring with the rebel Chen Xi, into a trap in which he was arrested and executed.

In 195 BCE Emperor Gaozu briefly imprisoned Xiao He for asking that parts of the imperial garden be given to peasants as farmland, then released him. Xiao He served Emperor Hui as chancellor until his death in 193 BCE and recommended Cao Shen as his successor, who kept his system unchanged. He is counted with Han Xin and Zhang Liang among the Three prominences of the early Han, and the Southern Qi and Liang dynasties were founded by his descendants Xiao Daocheng and Xiao Yan.
xiao-kui: Xiao Kui, courtesy name Renyuan, was born in 542 in the reign of his great-grandfather Emperor Wu of Liang. His father was Xiao Cha, Prince of Yueyang, and his mother was Xiao Cha's concubine Lady Cao. After the rebel general Hou Jing took the capital Jiankang in 549, Xiao Cha, fearing his uncle Xiao Yi, surrendered Yong Province to the Western Wei. When Western Wei forces defeated Xiao Yi, they made Xiao Cha emperor of Western Liang, a vassal holding little more than the land around Jiangling under a Western Wei commandant. Xiao Kui became crown prince after his elder brother Xiao Liao died, and succeeded in 562.

Xiao Kui was said to be learned, writing some 14 works on filial piety and on fortunetelling, and also highly superstitious; he was considered a capable administrator who let his war-weary subjects recover. In 567 he joined the Northern Zhou in aiding Hua Jiao, the Chen governor of Xiang Province, who had defected to them, but their forces were defeated at Dunkou by the Chen generals Chunyu Liang and Wu Mingche. In spring 568 Wu Mingche besieged Jiangling and tried to flood it; the city held out for over 100 days until Western Liang generals drove him off.

In 571, on Hua Jiao's advice, Emperor Wu of Northern Zhou gave the impoverished state three provinces, Ji, Ping and Ruo. In 577 Xiao Kui met Emperor Wu at Yecheng and won his favour by recalling, in tears, what his father had owed Yuwen Tai, and by comparing him to the mythical emperors Yao and Shun. In 580, when the general Yuchi Jiong rose against the regent Yang Jian, Xiao Kui took the advice of his official Liu Zhuang rather than most of his generals and sided with Yang.

Yang Jian founded the Sui dynasty in 581 as Emperor Wen. In 582 he asked for one of Xiao Kui's daughters as wife for his son Yang Guang, Prince of Jin; the diviners passed over the others and accepted a daughter born in the second month, thought an ill omen, who had been raised by her maternal uncle Zhang Ke. Emperor Wen then withdrew the Commandant of Jiangling. Xiao Kui paid homage at the new capital Daxing in spring 584 and died in summer 585; his son Xiao Cong succeeded him.
xiao-tong: Xiao Tong was born in the winter of 501 at Xiangyang to Xiao Yan, then a Southern Qi general close to victory in a civil war, and his concubine Ding Lingguang. In 502 Xiao Yan took the throne as Emperor Wu of Liang, and on 24 December 502, when Xiao Tong was one year old, he made him crown prince. His mother, though not made empress, was given a status equal to her son's. He married Lady Cai on 17 May 508 and was declared an adult on 31 January 515.

Like his father he became a devout Buddhist, studying the sutras and inviting monks to preach at his palace, and Emperor Wu gave him more and more matters of state. When his uncle Xiao Dan died in 522, he held that the custom sparing a crown prince from mourning an uncle was unfilial, and a one-month mourning set a precedent for the dynasty. With others he compiled the Wen Xuan, an anthology in 60 chapters whose 29th preserves the Nineteen Old Poems, a major source for early classical Chinese poetry.

His mother died on 3 January 527. When a Taoist monk warned that her burial ground would bring ill fortune to her eldest son, Xiao Tong let him bury wax geese there to avert it. An attendant later reported this to Emperor Wu as sorcery. The emperor executed only the monk, on the advice of the prime minister Xu Mian, but Xiao Tong never fully regained his father's trust.

Xiao Tong died in May 531, writing submissions to his father even while gravely ill. Emperor Wu buried him with an emperor's honours but, still resentful over the wax geese, passed over his son Xiao Huan and made his younger brother Xiao Gang crown prince. In 551 the rebel general Hou Jing deposed Xiao Gang and enthroned Xiao Tong's grandson Xiao Dong, and Xiao Tong was then honoured posthumously as an emperor. His son Xiao Cha later reigned as Emperor Xuan.
xiao-yanyan: Xiao Yanyan, also called Xiao Chuo, was the third child of Xiao Siwen, chancellor of the Liao, and the youngest of the Xiao sisters, after Xiao Hunian and Lady Xiao; her family's original Khitan name was Bali. She had first been betrothed to Han Derang, before the imperial clan intervened, and instead married Emperor Jingzong of Liao, to whom she bore the crown prince Yelü Longxu. As empress she was already influential during her husband's reign.

Jingzong died while returning from a hunting trip, and in 982 their son took the throne as Emperor Shengzong at the age of 12. Khitan custom allowed women to take part in war and to command armies, and she became a military commander of great renown. When the Song under Emperor Taizong invaded in 986, she commanded on the front line herself; the Song troops were routed and thousands captured, whom she pardoned because it was her birthday. A further Song invasion in 989 was also defeated, and the Song general Yang Ye was killed.

She commanded her own army of 10,000 cavalry and led the Liao army against the Song in person when she was over 50. She was also known for her skill in civil administration, and she arranged the marriage of her son to her court lady Xiao Noujin. She was on poor terms with her two older sisters and poisoned or murdered them both.

As regent she lived in an accepted, spouse-like relationship with Han Derang, her adviser and commander of the Northern Chancellery. The Song envoy Lu Zhen described her as about 50, wearing a kingfisher-feather cap and jade ear pendants and seated on a stack of cushions, attended by a dozen Khitan women; he saw a boy of about 10 who resembled Han and guessed he was their son. The History of the Khitan Kingdom says she had Han's wife poisoned and bore him a son.

She kept her influence until her death on 29 December 1009, and Chinese chronicles such as the History of the Liao credit her with most of the success of Shengzong's reign. She appears as an antagonist in many adaptations of the Generals of the Yang Family, and has been portrayed by Mu Qing in the film Great Liao's Empress Dowager (1995), by Shim Hye-jin in Empress Cheonchu (2009) and by Tiffany Tang in The Legend of Xiao Chuo (2020).
xicotencatl-the-elder: Xicotencatl was a teuctli, an elected official, of Tizatlan, one of the city-states of the Confederacy of Tlaxcala. By the time the Spaniards arrived he was very old and in poor health. The Tlaxcalan historian Diego Muñoz Camargo wrote that he was more than 120 years old and could see Hernán Cortés only if someone lifted his eyelids, and that he had more than 500 wives and concubines and many children, among them Xicotencatl II and Doña Lucía, the wife of Jorge de Alvarado.

The arrival of the Spaniards divided the Tlaxcalan senate. According to the chronicler Francisco Cervantes de Salazar, Maxixcatzin was open to an alliance, while Xicotencatl's son warned that the newcomers would make cruel masters. On the suggestion of Temilotecatl, Xicotencatl II and Otomi troops were allowed to attack Cortés, and when they were defeated Tlaxcala accepted the alliance. The Tlaxcalteca handed over 300 enslaved women, who were freed and baptised, and the lords of Tlaxcala married five of their own daughters to Spaniards: Xicotencatl's daughter Tecuelhuetzin married Pedro de Alvarado and was baptised María Luisa.

When Xicotencatl the Younger plotted to seize the lands of Chichimecatecuhtli during the Siege of Tenochtitlan, his father, by the account of Bernal Díaz del Castillo, told Cortés that his son was wicked and asked him to kill him, and Xicotencatl II was hanged. Xicotencatl converted to Christianity as Lorenzo Xicotencatl or Don Lorenzo de Vargas, and at his request one of his sons went with two other noblemen on an embassy to King Charles I of Spain. After his death nobles of the rival city-state of Ocotelolco took control of the confederacy.

One song or poem attributed to him survives in the Cantares mexicanos, a collection of Nahuatl songs probably compiled for Bernardino de Sahagún. It concerns the flower wars between Tlaxcala and the Aztec Triple Alliance.
xie-an: Xie An, courtesy name Anshi, was the son of the Jin minister Xie Pou. As a child he impressed the officials Huan Yi, Wang Meng and Wang Dao. After serving briefly as a low-level assistant to the chancellor he withdrew from government and repeatedly refused office, while teaching literature, philosophy and debate to his own children and those of his siblings; his favourite niece was the writer Xie Daoyun. Only after his brother Xie Wan was defeated in 359 and reduced to commoner status did he return, as an assistant to the general Huan Wen.

After Emperor Jianwen died in 372, Xie An joined Wang Tanzhi in denying Huan Wen the regency for the ten-year-old Emperor Xiaowu, inviting Empress Dowager Chu to serve instead. When Huan visited the capital in 373 amid rumours that he would kill them, Xie stayed calm and persuaded him to put away his display of troops. After Huan's death that year Xie divided his command among Huan Chong, Huan Huo and Huan Shixiu. With Wang Tanzhi's death in 375 he became in effect sole prime minister. He declared several general pardons and in 376 replaced the land tax with a head tax.

As Former Qin advanced, taking Xiangyang and Weixing in 379, Xie was said to calm the people by his own calm. In 383, as Fu Jiān attacked, he sent his brother Xie Shi to command, played Go with his nephew Xie Xuan before the battle, and returned troops Huan Chong had sent to the capital. On hearing of the victory at the Fei River he said only, "The kids won a battle."

After the battle his son-in-law Wang Guobao turned Emperor Xiaowu and his brother Sima Daozi against him. In 384 he declined to give Huan Chong's command to Xie Xuan and divided it within the Huan clan. He left the capital to avoid Sima Daozi and died soon after returning, ill, in 385. He was made Duke of Luling posthumously, and the Xie clan of Chen became one of the two most honoured clans of the Southern Dynasties.
xie-lingyun: Xie Lingyun descended from the Xie and Wang families, two of the leading houses of the later Eastern Jin. His paternal grandfather was the general Xie Xuan, who repelled the Former Qin at the Battle of Fei River, and his maternal grandmother was the only daughter of the calligrapher Wang Xizhi. Born in Yangxia County, he lost his father early and was brought up by the Buddhist monk Du Ming at Qiantang, now Hangzhou. He returned home in 399 and kept a Buddhist practice all his life. The family estate at Shining, laid out by his grandfather, held two hills with a lake between them.
During a major rebellion the family spent four years in the capital, Jiankang. The young duke, heir to a fief of three thousand households, became a figure of its social scene.

He served the Eastern Jin while the general Liu Yu put down the rebellion, but the Xie backed a rival general. When Liu Yu founded the Liu Song in 420, Xie was demoted to marquis with 500 households and posted to Yongjia, modern Wenzhou, where he wrote some of his finest poems. After a year he resigned, pleading ill health, and returned to Shining. There he explored the wild South Hill with dozens of servants, wearing wooden boots with spikes he could adjust for slopes, and his poems of this period were read in the capital.

Summoned to court in 426, he spent two years without real duty, returned in 430 to answer charges brought by his local prefect, and was sent in 431 to what is now Fuzhou in Jiangxi and the next year to Guangzhou. Sentenced to death in 433, he wrote a last poem lamenting that he would not die on one of his hilltops.

His poetry of mountains and streams is set apart from the poetry of fields and gardens; it is allusive and complex, possibly with Buddhist influence. Drawing on the fu tradition of eloquent descriptions of nature, in which he wrote his Fu on Returning to the Mountains, he compressed its essence into the shi form. The forty poems of the Wangchuan ji by Wang Wei and Pei Di, describing Wang Wei's Tang estate at Lantian, show his influence.
xie-xuan: Xie Xuan, courtesy name Youdu, was a scion of the influential Xie clan of Chen, the son of Xie Yi, elder brother of the prime minister Xie An; his sister Xie Daoyun was known for her literary talent and quick wit. Early in his career he and his uncle served on the staff of the paramount general Huan Wen, who prized his ability and predicted that by the age of forty he would hold a great general's banner. After Huan Wen's death in 373 he served under Huan Wen's brother Huan Huo.

In 377, when the court sought a general to defend the north-eastern border against Former Qin, Xie An recommended his nephew against the custom of not proposing one's own clan, and even his rival Xi Chao approved. Among Xie Xuan's recruits was Liu Laozhi, later his forward commander. In 379 he recaptured Pengcheng, defeating the Former Qin generals Ju Nan and Peng Chao, the first major Jin victory over Former Qin in decades.

In 383 his Beifu force served under his uncle Xie Shi. With the two armies stalemated across the Fei River, Xie Xuan asked the Former Qin commander Fu Rong to pull back so that the Jin troops could cross. The retreat turned to panic, Fu Rong was killed when his horse fell, and the Former Qin army collapsed under the attack of Xie Xuan, Xie Yan and Huan Yi.

For the victory he was made Duke of Kangle. In 384 he led a campaign to recover central China with Huan Shiqian, retaking most of the land south of the Yellow River and briefly relieving Fu Jiān's son Fu Pi, who was holding Yecheng against Murong Chui, founder of Later Yan. In 386, after the generals Zhai Liao and Zhang Yuan rebelled and opinion held that the troops were worn out, he gave up plans to go further and moved his headquarters south from Pengcheng to Huaiyin. Repeated illness led him to seek to resign, and he died in 388 as governor of Kuaiji Commandery, an important but mostly civilian post.
ximen-bao: Ximen Bao served Marquis Wen of Wei, who reigned from 445 to 396 BCE, as a minister and court adviser during the Warring States period. Around 400 BCE he was sent to the County of Ye, a poor district troubled by constant flooding. When he asked the people about their hardships, they named not the floods but the taxes raised every year to provide a bride for Hebo, the river god. Three powerful elders, the San Lao, had joined local officials and a shamaness in claiming that the floods were Hebo's anger; they kept most of the money, and a family that could not pay had its daughter taken and set adrift on the river.

On the day of the ceremony, before a crowd said to number over a thousand, Ximen declared the girl not beautiful enough for a god and ordered the rite postponed. He had the shamaness thrown into the river to tell Hebo, then her disciples and the three elders when none returned. When he ordered the officials and village elders to follow, they knelt in terror and promised to end the sacrifice, which was not held in Ye again.

Ximen then surveyed the land and had the people divert the river into 12 canals, which reduced the flow and watered the fields. The work was resented at first, but once it was finished the floods ceased and harvests doubled. He is also credited with a much larger scheme that diverted the Zhang River, which had joined the Yellow River at Anyang, to meet it further down near modern Tianjin, and so to irrigate the region of Henei with a contour canal. Work began between 403 and 387 BCE, and after setbacks, including local resistance to corvée labour, the engineer Shi Chi completed it a century later under King Xiang.

Ximen Bao is remembered as an early rationalist and as the first engineer in China to build a large canal irrigation system; the statesman Sunshu Ao, who dammed a river for an irrigation reservoir, is credited as China's first hydraulic engineer. The people of the district made a song in honour of the Zhang River diversion, recorded by the Han historian Ban Gu.
xin-dynasty: After the death of Emperor Wu of Han the ruling Liu family was beset by factional struggles, and the Wang family grew powerful under Emperor Cheng of Han. Its leading member, Wang Mang, acted as regent for several young puppet emperors and presented himself as a champion of Confucian virtues. After the death of Emperor Ping of Han in 6 CE he secured control of the empire and crushed rebellions in 6 and 7 CE. Two years later he usurped the throne and proclaimed the Xin dynasty, named for the fief of which he had been Marquess.

Wang Mang remade the Han government on his reading of the Confucian classics and of the ancient Western Zhou system. To weaken the nobles and help the peasants he redistributed land from the rich to those who owned none, limited the farmland a family could hold, taxed slave owning and prohibited the sale of slaves. He nationalised farmland, restored the state monopolies on salt and iron and replaced the gold currency with bronze. A 10% tax on the net earnings of gathering, fishing, herding and trade was abolished in 22 CE after it caused discontent.

Relations with the Xiongnu deteriorated, and Wang Mang kept 300,000 soldiers on the northern border, which drained the empire's resources. A change in the course of the Yellow River caused massive floods, and locust plagues and famines followed. Peasants in the east turned to banditry, and the strongest bands became the rebel armies known as the Red Eyebrows. They allied with discontented nobles and descendants of the Liu family, and by 19 CE there was a large-scale civil war.

Han restorationist armies completely defeated the Xin armies at the Battle of Kunyang in June or July 23 CE, and in October militias under Zhuang Ben and Zhuang Chun captured Chang'an and killed Wang Mang. In 25 CE Liu Xiu was crowned Emperor Guangwu of Han at Luoyang. He defeated the Red Eyebrows in 27 CE, and by 37 CE the Han dynasty was fully restored.
xinca-people: The Xinca, also written Xinka, live in southern Guatemala near the border with El Salvador and in the mountains to the north. Their Xincan languages are not known to be related to any other family, though they hold many loan words from the Mayan languages, and the Xinca may have been among the earliest inhabitants of south-eastern Guatemala, before the Maya and the Pipil arrived. Before the Spanish came in the early 16th century, the main Xinca territory lay east of the Pipil, in what is now the Santa Rosa Department, with further communities in Jutiapa.

At Guazacapán Pedro de Alvarado met a people who were neither Maya nor Pipil, probably the Xinca. With 250 Spanish infantry and 6,000 indigenous allies, mostly Kaqchikel and Cholultec, he took their chief city, Atiquipaque, usually placed near Taxisco, on 26 May 1524, after hand-to-hand fighting against warriors with spears, stakes and poisoned arrows; the Xinca population fell sharply. Survivors paid tribute in cacao, cotton, salt and vanilla, and many were enslaved and made to take part in the conquest of El Salvador, which gave the name Los Esclavos to a town, river and bridge near Cuilapa. After 1575 their removal to other regions hastened the decline of their culture and language.

The first pan-Xinka organisation, COPXIG, was founded at Chiquimulilla in 1994 and took part in negotiating the Accord on Indigenous Rights and Identities, signed in 1995, which named the Xinca among the peoples of the republic. A second body formed in 2002 became the country's first indigenous parliament. In the 2018 census 264,167 people, 1.8 per cent of the population, identified as Xinka, against 16,214 in 2002, a rise that followed a revivalist movement led by the two main Xinka political organisations.

In 2010 the Canadian company Tahoe Resources opened the Escobal mine at San Rafael Las Flores on Xinca land. During protests against it in March 2013 four Xinca community leaders were kidnapped and one was killed, and the Xinca then blockaded the roads at Casillas to stop supplies reaching the mine. Guatemala's Constitutional Court halted its operation, and in April 2018 at least 2,000 Xinca marched in Guatemala City demanding its closure.
xing-ware: Xing ware, Xingyao in Chinese, takes its name from Xingzhou in southern Hebei, and kiln sites have been found in Neiqiu County and in Lincheng. White ceramics were made there from the Northern dynasties period, the early wares coarser, and production reached its peak under the Tang dynasty. The thin white body of the finest pieces needed no slip, while coarser pieces have a layer of white slip. A thin clear glaze, often with a bluish tinge, contains magnesium oxide and phosphorus pentoxide, which reduce dripping and cracking. Some early pieces have green glaze and later ones yellow or black glaze or sancai.

The kilns were fired with wood, and saggars protected the wares. Many pieces are not quite vitrified enough to be translucent and would count as stoneware by Western definition, but some are true porcelain, and Xing ware may therefore be considered the world's first true porcelain. Chinese usage makes no such distinction and calls it porcelain.

Xing ware was used at the Tang court: sherds marked Ying, for an imperial storehouse, or Hanlin have been found at the Daming Palace and at the kilns. In The Classic of Tea, Lu Yu contrasted white Xing ware with the green Yue ware of the south and compared its colours to snow and silver, and white ware came to be linked with the north. The scholar Li Zhao wrote that the Xing ware of Neiqiu was used by rich and poor alike. It was exported too: pieces were found in the Belitung shipwreck, and finds in Iraq are common enough to be called the Samarra type.

Ding ware, made nearby at Dingzhou, seems to have begun by imitating Xing ware and can be hard to tell from it, though Xing ware may have a colder, bluer tone. Ding eclipsed Xing during the Five Dynasties and replaced it under the Song. The kilns were not located until 1980 and 1981, when sites were excavated at Ciqun in Lincheng County, and later excavations found many more in Neiqiu and Xingtai.
xingtai: Xingtai is a prefecture-level city in southern Hebei province, formerly known as Xingzhou or Shunde. It covers 12,486 km2 and borders Shijiazhuang and Hengshui to the north, Handan to the south, Shandong to the east and Shanxi to the west. The climate is continental and semi-arid, with hot, humid summers, cold, windy and very dry winters, and spring sandstorms blowing in from the Mongolian steppe. The city's rainfall averages 496.5 mm a year, more than half of it falling in July and August.

The history of Xingtai is traced back 3,500 years. It served as a capital under the Shang dynasty, and under the Zhou dynasty the State of Xing, from which the present name derives, was founded there. During the Warring States period the state of Zhao made it a provisional capital. It was known as Xindu for most of the Qin dynasty, but after the Battle of Julu in 207 BCE it became Xiangguo. When Shi Le of the Jie founded the Later Zhao in the Sixteen Kingdoms period, the capital was again at Xiangguo. Under the Sui and Tang it was called Xingzhou, and under the Yuan, Ming and Qing it was Shunde, a prefecture.

In Sui, Tang and Song times the area was the most prolific ceramics centre of northern China, rivalling the Yue ware of the south. The white ware and new techniques of the Xing kiln mark the transition from proto-porcelain to true porcelain. More than thirty kiln sites have been excavated in the city's districts. On 8 March 1966 an earthquake of magnitude 6.8, with its epicentre in Longyao County, struck the area, followed by five quakes above magnitude 6 until 29 March. It caused 8,064 deaths and destroyed more than 5 million houses.

At the 2020 census Xingtai had 7,111,106 inhabitants, and it administers 4 districts, 2 county-level cities and 12 counties. It is a base for natural resources in North China, producing 20 million metric tonnes of coal annually, and four railways and five expressways serve it.
xingyang: Xingyang lies about 15 kilometres west of Zhengzhou city proper, under whose administration it falls, and its Wangcun Town stands on the flat southern bank of the Yellow River. Its name, taken from the Shangshu, means the city north of the Xing River, and its history can be traced in books written more than 3,000 years ago.

Chinese legend holds that Xingyang is where Chang'e flew to the Moon. People from Xingyang include Shen Buhai, a legalist of the Warring States period, and Li Shangyin, a poet of the late Tang dynasty, and it is considered the place of origin of the Zheng surname. Remains of the Yangshao culture and of the Han dynasty, and Buddhist antiquities, have been found there.
