At Chuhehanjie, also called Honggou, Liu Bang, founder of the Western Han dynasty, and his rival Xiang Yu fought for years without either winning, and agreed to divide China, the east to Xiang Yu and the west to Liu Bang. Liu Bang broke the agreement when Xiang Yu withdrew from Xingyang to relieve his capital, which Han Xin had attacked. The border between them is still recalled as the divider on the board of Xiangqi, Chinese chess. The Hulao Pass, where Lü Bu fought Liu Bei, Guan Yu and Zhang Fei in the Three Kingdoms period, is also in Xingyang.

Xingyang is a county-level city of around 590,000 people over about 908 square kilometres, divided into 16 township-level divisions. Zhengzhou West Railway Station and several stations of the Zhengzhou Metro lie within it. The pond systems of Wangcun Town, developed since 1986, made it the largest aquaculture centre in North China.
xinhai-revolution: The revolution came after a decade of agitation, revolts and uprisings. The Qing had struggled to reform and to resist foreign aggression since its defeat in the First Opium War in 1842, and defeat by Japan in 1895 convinced many of the need for institutional change. The Guangxu Emperor's Hundred Days' Reform of 1898 was cancelled by a conservative coup led by the Empress Dowager Cixi. After 1900 conservatives at court thought the reforms too radical, and reformers thought them too slow. Anti-Manchu feeling, which had never entirely disappeared, fed the revolutionaries.

The flashpoint came on 10 October 1911 with the Wuchang Uprising by members of the New Army, after some Hubei units were sent to Sichuan to put down the Railway Protection Movement, a mass protest against the seizure of local railway ventures and their handover to foreign powers. Similar revolts followed, among them Changsha on 22 October, Taiyuan on 29 October, Kunming on 30 October and Shanghai on 3 November, and in the end every province renounced the Qing. Violence against Manchus occurred in several places. In Xi'an, after the Manchu quarter fell on 24 October, about 20,000 Manchus in the city were killed.

On 1 November the Qing court appointed Yuan Shikai prime minister. Revolutionary forces took Nanjing on 2 December, and a North–South Conference met in Shanghai on 18 December. On 29 December Sun Yat-sen was elected provisional president, and 1 January 1912 became the first day of the first year of the Republic of China.

Sun agreed to resign in favour of Yuan if Yuan secured the emperor's abdication. The edict of abdication of the six-year-old emperor was promulgated on 12 February 1912, and Yuan was sworn in as provisional president on 10 March. Song Jiaoren, who led the Kuomintang to a majority in the first National Assembly elections, was assassinated in Shanghai on 20 March 1913 under a secret order by Yuan. Yuan proclaimed himself emperor in December 1915 but abdicated in March 1916 after strong opposition, and his death in June 1916 was followed by decades of warlordism.

The revolution ended over two millennia of imperial rule in China. Tibet and Outer Mongolia took the fall of the dynasty as dissolving their allegiance, and Bogd Khan became ruler of the Bogd Khanate on 29 December 1911. 10 October is the National Day of the Republic of China on Taiwan and the Anniversary of the 1911 Revolution in China.
xining: Xining lies in the valley of the Huangshui River, a tributary of the Yellow River, at an average altitude of about 2,200 metres on the eastern edge of the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau. It is about 200 km west of Lanzhou and stood on the traditional main trade route from northern China into Tibet and the Qaidam Basin. It was a commercial hub on the Hexi Corridor caravan route, handling especially timber, wool and salt in ancient times, as part of the Northern Silk Road, whose use grew in the 1st century BCE after Han efforts to control it.

Under the Han dynasty a county called Linqiang was set up to control the local Qiang tribesmen. It was a frontier county again under the Sui and Tang, and in the 7th and early 8th centuries a centre of constant warfare with the Tuyuhun and Tibet. The Tibetans overran it in 763, and the Chinese knew it under Tibetan control as Qingtang. The Song dynasty recovered it in 1104 and named it Xining, meaning peace in the west; it has been the seat of a prefecture or superior prefecture under that name since then.

Tsongkhapa, founder of the Gelug school, was born in the region, and Kumbum Monastery was founded at his birthplace in the late 16th century, making Xining an important centre for the Gelug school. A magnitude 7.6 earthquake on 22 May 1927 killed over 40,000 people. Xining stayed in Gansu until 1928, when it became capital of the new province of Qinghai. Japanese aircraft bombed it in 1941, and the Salar general Han Youwen directed its defence. It received municipal status in 1945. Under Governor Ma Bufang it was industrialised and modernised, and the rail link to Lanzhou, completed in 1959, spurred industry.

Xining is the capital and most populous city of Qinghai and the largest city on the Tibetan Plateau, with about 2.5 million inhabitants at the 2020 census. Only about four of its roughly 37 nationalities are numerically significant: the Han, Hui, Monguor or Tu, and Tibetans. Kumbum Monastery, one of six leading monasteries of the Gelug school, lies to the south-west, and the Dongguan Mosque, over 600 years old, is one of the best known in north-west China. A railway reaches Lhasa, opened in 2006, and the city has a cool summer climate, which has earned it the name Summer Resort Capital of China.
xinjiang: Xinjiang is split by the Tian Shan mountain range into the Dzungarian Basin in the north and the Tarim Basin in the south. The Karakoram, Kunlun and Tian Shan ranges occupy much of its borders and its western and southern regions. Most of it is uninhabitable desert and dry grassland, and only about 9.7 per cent of the land is fit for habitation, mostly in oases at the foot of the mountains, where the cities lie. Its older English-language names include Chinese Turkestan and East Turkestan, and the Chinese called it Xiyu, the Western Regions.

Crossed by the Northern Silk Road, the Tarim and Dzungaria were known as the Western Regions. At the start of the Han dynasty the region was ruled by the Xiongnu. In the 2nd century BCE Emperor Wu of Han sent Zhang Qian west to seek an alliance with the Yuezhi, and in 60 BCE the Han established the Protectorate of the Western Regions at Wulei. The area, once inhabited by Indo-European Tocharians and Iranian Sakas who followed Buddhism and Zoroastrianism, became Muslim in the 10th century with the conversion of the Kara-Khanid Khanate, which held Kashgar.

The Uyghur state of the Turpan-Urumchi region submitted to Genghis Khan in 1209, and Xinjiang later came under Kaidu, a descendant of Ögedei Khan. In the 18th century the Qing fought the Dzungars for decades; Qing Manchu Bannermen then carried out the Dzungar genocide, nearly eradicating them and depopulating Dzungaria, and by 1759 China controlled both Dzungaria and the Tarim Basin. The two were governed separately until 1884, when the Qing established the province of Xinjiang. After the fall of the Qing in 1912, Yang Zengxin ruled it for the Republic of China until 1928. The region became part of the People's Republic of China in 1949 and an autonomous region in 1955.

Xinjiang, officially the Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, is the largest province-level division of China, covering more than 1.6 million square kilometres in the northwest. It is home to the Uyghurs, Han Chinese, Hui, Kazakhs, Kyrgyz, Mongols and other peoples, with several autonomous prefectures and counties for minorities. Its largest cities include Ürümqi, Turpan, Kashgar and Karamay, and it has substantial oil and mineral reserves.
xinzheng: Xinzheng (simplified Chinese 新郑, traditional 新鄭, pinyin Xīnzhèng) is a county-level city of Henan Province, China. It is administered by the prefecture-level city of Zhengzhou, the provincial capital. It has a population of about 600,000 and covers 873 square kilometres, of which 15 square kilometres are urban. Its local economy rests on agriculture and heavy industry. Farmers grow maize, cotton, tobacco and other industrial crops, and the city is known for its jujube, the Chinese date, which is sold at harvest in the markets and along the roads into town. Cigarette factories stand near the centre, and coal mining has also been an important source of income.

Xinzheng is considered one of the birthplaces of the Chinese nation. More than 8,000 years ago Neolithic people of the Peiligang culture lived in the vicinity. The Yellow Emperor of tradition is said to have been born at Xinzheng about 5,000 years ago, and the nearby Shizu mountain is said to be the exact place of his birth. During the Zhou dynasty Xinzheng was the capital of the state of Zheng and, after the conquest of Zheng by the state of Han, of Han as well. Historically the district formed part of Zhengzhou. In 1994 the Henan Provincial Council authorised its incorporation as a separate municipality.

Zhengzhou Xinzheng International Airport, which serves the provincial capital, lies in Xinzheng and is the only international airport of Henan. The city has two large private universities, Sias International University and ShengDa University, whose students and teachers have shaped local services such as housing, restaurants and shops. Each spring the city hosts a ceremony honouring the Yellow Emperor, held to be an ancestor of the Chinese nation; in 2009 it drew over 10,000 visitors from within China and from overseas Chinese communities. Investors began a large concrete dragon along the ridge of Shizu mountain in the early 21st century, but it was left unfinished for lack of funding. Xinzheng is described as an open-air museum.
xiongnu-empire: The Mongolian Plateau of central and eastern Mongolia was earlier inhabited by the Slab Grave Culture, which lasted until the 3rd century BCE. The language of the Xiongnu is disputed, and Turkic, Iranian, Mongolic and Yeniseian origins have all been proposed.

Their first known leader, Touman, reigned between 220 and 209 BCE. In 215 BCE Emperor Qin Shi Huang sent General Meng Tian against the Xiongnu, who drove them from the Ordos Loop and forced them to flee north into the Mongolian Plateau. In 209 BCE Touman's son Modu became chanyu.

In the winter of 200 BCE, after a Xiongnu siege of Taiyuan, Emperor Gaozu of Han led a campaign against Modu and was ambushed at the Battle of Baideng, where he was cut off from supplies for seven days and narrowly escaped capture. Later the Han emperor Wu sent Zhang Qian west to seek an alliance with the Yuezhi against the Xiongnu. The mission failed, but his reports prompted Han preparations to break the Xiongnu hold on the westward routes.

When the chanyu Xulüquanqu died in 60 BCE, a succession dispute began that lasted until 53 BCE. In that year Huhanye moved south and submitted to the Han, entering tributary relations in which he was to pay homage, send a hostage prince and present tribute. His brother Zhizhi moved west and was killed by a Chinese army in 36 BCE near Lake Balkhash. A second succession quarrel around 47 CE left the Xiongnu divided into southern and northern groups. Those who resettled within the Great Wall gradually intermixed with the Han, and by the 7th century the Xiongnu had completely integrated into Chinese society.

The ruler was the chanyu, and below him stood the tuqi kings, of whom the Tuqi King of the Left was normally the heir. Beneath them were officials in left and right pairs and commanders of detachments of a thousand, a hundred and ten men, so that the nation was organised like an army. A weakness was the custom of lateral succession, in which a dead ruler's brother took power if his son was too young. The Xiongnu herded flocks and traded horses with China, and ate mostly mutton, horse meat and wild geese. According to the Book of Han they called Heaven Chēnglí, a transcription of Tengri.
xipe-totec: The origin of Xipe Totec is uncertain. He was widely worshipped in central Mexico at the time of the Spanish Conquest and was known through most of Mesoamerica; representations have been found as far away as Tazumal in El Salvador. His worship was common along the Gulf Coast in the Early Postclassic, and he probably became an important Aztec god after the Aztec conquest of the Gulf Coast in the middle of the fifteenth century.

The name joins xīpe, flayed, with totēc, the first-person plural possessive of tēuctli, lord. He was also called Tlatlauhqui Tezcatlipoca, Red Smoking Mirror, Yohuallahuan, the Night Drinker, and Yaotzin, revered enemy. The Tlaxcaltecs and Huexotzincas worshipped a version of him as Camaxtli. In January 2019 archaeologists of Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History confirmed the first known surviving temple of the god, in Puebla, built by the Popoluca between 1000 and 1260 CE.

In Aztec belief Xipe Totec was a god of life, death and rebirth, of agriculture, vegetation, the east, spring, goldsmiths and silversmiths, and of warfare, which he was believed to have invented. He was said to have flayed himself to feed humanity, as maize seeds lose their outer layer before germinating and snakes shed their skin.

His insignia, the pointed cap and rattle staff, were the war attire of the Mexica emperor, and his temple, the Yopico, stood within the Great Temple of Tenochtitlan. He was also linked to pimples, inflammations, eye diseases and smallpox, and offerings were made to him by the sick. He is shown wearing flayed human skin, often painted yellow on one side, with the skin of the hands hanging loose from the wrists.

His festival, Tlacaxipehualiztli, literally the flaying of men, was held at the spring equinox before the rains, in March at the time of the Spanish Conquest. Its central act was the gladiatorial sacrifice of war prisoners, in which a captive tied to a large round stone fought an armed Aztec warrior.

The bodies were flayed, and priests and warriors wore the skins for twenty days, an act called Neteotquiliztli, the impersonation of a god. Wearers went through the city begging alms and blessing those who gave. People also touched the skins to relieve illness. Afterwards the skins were stored in lidded containers in a chamber beneath the temple. Goldsmiths held their own feast of Yopico in the same month.
xishuangbanna: Xishuangbanna lies in the extreme south of Yunnan, on the northern edge of the tropics, bordering Myanmar and Laos. The prefectural seat, Jinghong, is the largest settlement and straddles the Mekong, called the Lancang River in Chinese. The prefecture lies at a lower altitude than most of Yunnan, with a tropical savanna climate. The name Sibsongpanna is a Tai Lue compound of sipsong, twelve, pan, township, and na, rice paddy, and refers to the traditional division of the mueang into twelve districts. Its people, architecture and language resemble those of the Shan, Dai and Tai peoples, including the Thai and Lao, more than those of the Han Chinese.

Before 1886 the region was called Chiang Hung, a Tai Lue kingdom contended between China, Lanna and the Burmese dynasties. After the Mongol conquest in 1296, the Ming and Qing emperors appointed the Tai Lue rulers as native Tusi governors. In 1563 King Bayinnaung of Burma captured Chiang Hung, and Burma and China then agreed on joint domination, the ruler being enthroned at a ceremony that Burmese and Chinese representatives jointly presided over. In the 19th century it briefly became a tributary of Luang Prabang and the Rattanakosin Kingdom during the Burmese-Siamese War of 1849-1855. When the British Empire occupied Upper Burma in 1886 it became part of the British Raj, and in 1892 the British transferred Chiang Hung to the Qing dynasty.

The Republic of China sent troops in 1913 to oust a local rebel, the Chao Maha of Meng Jie, and Ke Shuxun governed under his 13 Principles of Governing the Frontier. The Communists took control in 1952. On 23 January 1953 the People's Republic established the Xishuangbanna Dai Autonomous Region and ended the native-chieftain system, and in 1955 it became an autonomous prefecture. Land reform began in January 1956. Buddhist temples used as barns in the Cultural Revolution were restored to their purpose in 1981.

The prefecture is the home of the Dai people. A New Tai Lue alphabet, based on the Tai Tham alphabet, was created in 1953 to print material in Tai Lue. The Dai New Year, the Water-Splashing Festival, runs from 13 to 15 April. The region holds much of the biodiversity of Yunnan and the last few Asian elephants in China, protected in a reserve. Its six tea mountains produce Pu-erh tea.
xochitecatl: The site lies 18 km southwest of Tlaxcala city on the summit of an extinct volcano 4 km wide, which rises about 200 metres above the floor of the Puebla-Tlaxcala Valley. From it there are clear views to the volcanoes Popocatepetl, Iztaccihuatl and La Malinche, and the rivers Atoyac and Zahuapan flow nearby through fertile farmland. Cacaxtla lies 1 km to the east. The ruins cover 12 hectares, arranged around two plazas: the Pyramid of Flowers, the Serpent Building and the Platform of the Volcanoes stand on the main plaza, and the circular Spiral Building borders the western one. The name joins the Nahuatl words for flower and person.

Building began around 800 BCE with the Pyramid of Flowers, the Spiral Building and the Serpent Building. Between 350 BCE and 100 CE Xochitecatl was the centre of a powerful chiefdom controlling much of western Tlaxcala, and it seems to have been a purely ceremonial centre for people living dispersed in the countryside rather than a town. The site was abandoned in about 150 CE, after an eruption of Popocatepetl. The Spiral Building, a stepped pyramid with no stairway, was climbed by following its own spiral, and was probably a temple to Ehecatl, the god of wind.

Between 600 and 950 CE parts of the site were reused as a secondary ceremonial centre of Cacaxtla. The Platform of the Volcanoes was built, and the Pyramid of Flowers, whose base of 100 by 140 metres is close to that of the Pyramid of the Moon at Teotihuacan, became the focus of rites that included the sacrifice of children: more than 30 children were buried in it. On its stairway lay more than 2,000 clay figurines, most of them women of every age, among them pregnant women and mothers carrying children. Both sites were abandoned around 950, though rites continued in the Postclassic.

Mari Carmen Serra Puche led the main excavations from 1993, which uncovered two obsidian workshops in the Pyramid of Flowers and the Serpent Building. A Christian cross placed on the Spiral Building in 1632 still stands. The site is in the care of the Instituto Nacional de Antropología e Historia and is open to the public.
xoybun: Xoybûn, or Khoybun, was founded on 5 October 1927 at Bhamdoun in Greater Lebanon, at a congress of Kurdish notables drawn from the Society for the Elevation of Kurdistan, Azadî, the Kürt Teşkilat-ı İçtimaiye Cemiyeti and the Kürt Millet Fırkası. Among those present were Kamuran Bedir Khan, Celadet Bedir Khan, Memduh Selim, Haco Agha and Mehdi Saïd, brother of Sheikh Said. It presented itself as progressive but pragmatic, aiming at independence and wanting to learn from the failure of the Sheikh Said rebellion.

Celadet Alî Bedirxan was elected president, and the first central committee included Memduh Selim, Mehmet Şükrü Sekban, Haco Agha, Ali Rıza and Süleymniyeli Kerim Rüstem Bey. The league had an armed section, led by Ihsan Nuri, a former Ottoman soldier, and a political one, based in Damascus and represented in several western countries, mostly by members of the Bedirxan family. Many Armenians joined, and on 29 October 1927 a treaty with the Armenian Revolution Federation (Dashnaktsutyun) was negotiated in Beirut by Vahan Papazian for the ARF and by Celadet Bedir Khan and others for Xoybûn. It stood as a counterweight to the SAK of Seyyit Abdul Kadir, which sought autonomy rather than independence.

The leadership promoted Ihsan Nuri to the rank of general and sent him to Erzurum with 20 comrades, and the league published a newspaper, Agirî. The Republic of Ararat declared its independence on 8 October 1927 or 1928. The central committee named Ibrahim Heski, a chieftain of the Jalali tribe, governor of Agirî Province and Ihsan Nuri Pasha general commander of the Kurdish armed forces.

Xoybûn appealed to the Great Powers and the League of Nations, but under Turkish pressure the British Empire and France restricted its members' activities, and Turkey's opposition led to the closure of its work in Aleppo in 1928. Turkey repeatedly accused Kurdish and Armenian rebels of crossing into the country to assassinate Mustafa Kemal. After Turkish forces put down the Ararat rebellion, the league remained active across Kurdistan until it was dissolved in 1946.
xu-da: Xu Da, courtesy name Tiande, was a friend of Zhu Yuanzhang, the future Hongwu Emperor. He was described as a stalwart man with a slim face and high cheekbones. In 1353 he joined the Red Turban rebels against the Mongol-led Yuan dynasty and served as a general under Zhu Yuanzhang, helping him defeat rival warlords and other opposing forces. He was known as a cautious commander, skilled in governing an army.

In 1368, the year the Ming dynasty was founded, Xu Da and other Ming generals attacked Khanbaliq, present-day Beijing, and forced the last Yuan ruler, Toghon Temür, to flee north. Xu Da pursued the retreating Yuan forces into Mongol territory, routed Mongol reinforcements, sacked the Mongol capital at Karakorum and in 1370 captured thousands of Mongol nobles. His army went on to Transbaikalia, further north than any Chinese army had gone before. Zhu Yuanzhang praised him as the Great Wall of the Ming, and he held the title Duke of Wei.

Xu Da's family married into the imperial house. His eldest daughter, Xu Yihua, married Zhu Di, the emperor's fourth son, and became Empress Renxiaowen when he reigned as the Yongle Emperor; two other daughters married the princes of Dai and An. Xu Da was the maternal grandfather of the Hongxi Emperor, and all but two of the later Ming and Southern Ming emperors descended from him.

Xu Da fell ill with a carbuncle in 1384 and died of illness in 1385. Unlike many generals who had helped found the Ming, he was never accused of plotting against the Hongwu Emperor. A later legend says that the emperor, knowing him to be allergic to goose, sent him a goose dish and had him made to eat it; the story arose after his death, and contemporary sources describe the two men as close until the end. He was posthumously made Prince of Zhongshan and given the first place in the Imperial Ancestral Temples and the Portrait Temples of Meritorious Officials.
xu-guangqi: Xu Guangqi was born in Shanghai, then a small walled county seat in Songjiang Prefecture, on 24 April 1562. His branch of the Xu clan was not related to those that had passed the imperial examinations and joined the local gentry. His father, Xu Sicheng, had been orphaned at five and lost most of his inheritance to pirate raids and insolvent friends. By the time Xu was six the family had saved enough to send him to a local school, and from 1569 to 1573 he attended the school at the Buddhist monastery at Longhua. His mother died on 8 May 1592, and after the mourning period he seems to have failed the provincial examination in 1594.

In 1596 Xu moved to Xunzhou in Guangxi to assist its prefect, and he passed the provincial examination at Beijing the next year, but failed the imperial examination. He turned to military and agricultural subjects and studied under Cheng Jiasui. After meeting Matteo Ricci at Nanjing in 1600 he collaborated with him on translations of Western texts into Chinese and of Confucian texts into Latin. Ricci's influence led to his baptism in 1603. From 1607 to 1610 he was forced to retire and experimented at home with Western-style irrigation and with sweet potatoes, cotton and the nu zhen tree.

In 1629 his memorials persuaded the court to let the Portuguese captain Gonçalo Teixeira-Correa bring ten artillery pieces and four bombards to the capital. The guns were sent to Dengzhou in Shandong, where his protégé Ignatius Sun was governor. After a mutiny under Kong Youde and Geng Zhongming captured Dengzhou in 1632, Xu's pleas for clemency failed and Sun was court-martialled and executed. He rose to be Minister of Rites and Deputy Senior Grand Secretary.

Besides the Euclid translation and the calendar reform, Xu wrote a book on military techniques, Mr Xu's Amateur Observations, and put forward the concept of a Rich Country and Strong Army, which Japan later adopted as Fukoku Kyohei. His Complete Treatise on Agriculture followed Wang Zhen and Jia Sixie and was seven times as long as either. It treated irrigation, fertilisers, famine relief, economic crops and empirical observation. The Chongzhen calendar introduced European mathematics and astronomy to China, with the Tychonic system as its theoretical basis.

Xu died on 8 November 1633. Johann Adam Schall von Bell stayed with him in his final illness and oversaw the return of his body to Shanghai, where it was buried in 1641. His tomb is the centrepiece of Guangqi Park.
xu-shouhui: Xu Shouhui, also known as Xu Zhenyi, was born in Luotian, in present-day Hubei, and worked as a cloth vendor. In August 1351 he and others at Qízhōu raised a rebel army of Red Turbans under the pretence of the Buddhist White Lotus Society, as part of the Red Turban Rebellion against the Yuan dynasty.

In the following months the rebels captured Qishui, which became the command centre of the Red Turbans and the capital of the new empire, first called Song and then Tianwan, with Xu as its emperor under the era name Zhiping. His following grew quickly as he claimed to be the Maitreya Buddha, who sought to destroy the rich to benefit the poor. In 1352 his forces moved on to take Jiangxi, Anhui, Fujian, Zhejiang, Jiangsu and Hunan.

After a temporary defeat by the army of the Yuan he fled to Huangmei Mountain, but he returned in 1355 to campaign again and moved his capital to Hanyang. In 1358 his officer Chen Youliang took the city of Longxing, now Nanchang, and Xu wished to move his capital there. Chen opposed the plan, since Longxing lay not far from his own base at Jiangzhou and Xu's presence would threaten him.

Xu insisted, and in December 1359 he ordered his troops to sail down the Yangtze River to Jiangzhou. Chen Youliang had expected this and laid an ambush. When Xu arrived, Chen detained him, killed the rest of his men and proclaimed himself King of the State of Han. Xu remained in Chen's captivity until his death in 1360.
xu-shuzheng: Xu Shuzheng was born on 11 November 1880 in Xiao County, Jiangsu, now part of Anhui, into a family of scholars, and was one of the youngest people ever to pass the imperial examinations. In 1905 he entered the Japanese School of Land Army Officials, returning to China in 1910. From 1911 to 1917 he held staff posts in the First Army, rising to chief of land forces, and in 1914 he founded the Cheng Da Middle School.

Xu was the right-hand man of Duan Qirui. In 1918 he founded the Anfu Club, the political arm of the Anhui clique, which went on to win three-fourths of the seats in the National Assembly. The same year he executed Lu Jianzhang, having found that Lu was trying to persuade his nephew Feng Yuxiang to turn against the Anhui clique.

In 1919 Xu took command of the Northwest Frontier Defense Army, which invaded the newly independent Outer Mongolia in October, and on 17 November he forced it to withdraw its declaration of autonomy. When Duan fell in 1920 Xu lost his post and was replaced in Mongolia by Chen Yi; early in 1921 Mongolia became independent again after the Russian-Mongol army of Baron Roman von Ungern-Sternberg defeated the Chinese forces. Xu's troops lost the Zhili-Anhui War, and he took shelter in the Japanese embassy.
In the early 1920s he was sent to Italy with a Chinese diplomatic mission, in part to get him out of the country, and he came back in 1924 when Duan returned as chief executive.

In December 1925, travelling by train from Beijing to Shanghai, Xu was kidnapped by Zhang Zhijiang of Feng Yuxiang's forces and killed at dawn the next day, on 29 December, at the age of 45, in revenge for Lu Jianzhang. His death also deprived Feng's rival Duan of a powerful supporter. His third son, Hsu Dau-lin, published a biography of him in Chinese in 1962, The Life of General Hsu Shu-tseng.
xu-wen: Xu Wen was born in 862, in the reign of Emperor Yizong of Tang, to a family from Qushan, in modern Lianyungang. His parents' names are lost, though his mother is known to have been surnamed Zhou, and as a young man he was a salt privateer. He became a soldier under Yang Xingmi, then prefect of Lu Prefecture, but was not counted among Yang's 36 distinguished officers. When Yang took Xuan Prefecture in 889, he alone of the officers looked for food rather than spoils and had porridge given to the hungry.

In 895 he took into his household a seven-year-old boy captured at Hao Prefecture, whom Yang Wo disliked, named him Xu Zhigao and had his second wife, Lady Li, raise him. In 902 his warning that silted canals would stop large supply ships proved right, and Yang gave him greater responsibility.

Under Yang Xingmi's son Yang Wo, Xu Wen and Zhang Hao took control of the headquarters by force in 907 and later had Yang Wo killed. Xu then had the officer Zhong Taizhang kill Zhang, blamed the murder on Zhang alone and became regent for Yang Longyan as sole commander of the guards. He left military affairs to Yan Keqiu and finances to Luo Zhixiang, and though illiterate he ruled on legal cases after having the papers read to him. In 909 he sent Xu Zhigao to command the fleet at Jinling, and in 910 Yang Longyan accepted the title of Prince of Wu, by which the state was afterwards known.

Under Yang Pu, Xu Wen had the ruler sacrifice to Heaven in 921, in a more frugal form than the Tang ceremonies, and in 923 he decided against joining Later Tang in its war on Later Liang. His eldest son, Xu Zhixun, was killed by Zhu Jin in 918. Xu Wen died on 20 November 927 and Xu Zhigao inherited his place as regent. After founding the Southern Tang, Xu Zhigao honoured him posthumously as Emperor Wu, with the temple name Yizu.
xuantu-commandery: Xuantu was one of the Four Commanderies of Han, set up in 107 BCE in the northern Korean Peninsula and part of the Liaodong Peninsula after the Han dynasty conquered Wiman Chosŏn. Its first seat was Fort Okjeo. In 82 BCE, when the Han reduced the number of its commandery units, the Lintun Commandery was merged into Xuantu.

In 75 BCE raids by the Maek tribes, probably a reference to Gaogouli, forced Xuantu to move its seat from Fort Okjeo to Gaogouli County in Liaodong. Several of its former counties were abandoned or reassigned, seven of them to the Lelang Commandery as the so-called seven counties beyond the eastern pass, which left Xuantu with only three: Gaogouli, Shangyintai and Xigaima. The Book of Han records 45,006 households and 221,845 people in the commandery in 2 CE.

By the time General Sima Yi of Cao Wei defeated Gongsun Yuan in his campaign against Liaodong in 238, the commandery had retreated further west, to the area of present-day Fushun, and held four counties: Gaogouli, Gaoxian, Liaoyang and Wangping. Goguryeo conquered it in 319 CE.

Where the commanderies lay has become a matter of dispute. In North Korean scholarship, and in part of South Korean scholarship, the Han annexation of parts of the peninsula is denied, and the Four Commanderies are placed outside it, in the Liaodong Commandery; on this view Xuantu lay at Shenyang. The theory is authoritative in North Korea and has support among amateur historians in South Korea, but it is not recognised in the academic circles of the United States, China and Japan.
xuanwu-gate-incident: Li Jiancheng, Emperor Gaozu's eldest son, was heir apparent, but his younger brother Li Shimin won greater prestige by defeating Dou Jiande and Wang Shichong, while Li Jiancheng guarded the northern frontier against the Tujue. Placed over the eastern plain from Luoyang, Li Shimin appointed about fifty officials and in 621 founded a College of Literary Studies of eighteen scholars. In Chang'an, Li Jiancheng recruited more than two thousand Changlin troops and allied with Prince Li Yuanji, with the support of the emperor's consorts.

The rivalry deepened after Yang Wengan's rebellion of 624, when Gaozu first offered Li Shimin the succession but left Li Jiancheng as heir after his supporters interceded. Some texts say the two brothers tried to poison Li Shimin, though when or whether this happened is disputed; they did secure the dismissal of his advisers Fang Xuanling and Du Ruhui.

In early 626 Li Yuanji was given command against the Tujue, with Li Shimin's best generals and troops, and Li Shimin heard that his brothers planned to kill him when he saw Li Yuanji off. Advised by Zhangsun Wuji, Fang Xuanling, Du Ruhui, Yuchi Jingde and Hou Junji, he bribed Chang He, commander of the Xuanwu Gate, and accused his brothers before Gaozu of affairs with the emperor's consorts. Warned by Consort Zhang, the princes rode to the palace at dawn on 2 July 626 to answer the charge.

Near the Linhu Hall they sensed the ambush and turned back. Li Shimin shot Li Jiancheng dead; Yuchi Jingde's seventy horsemen brought down Li Yuanji, who, after Li Shimin fell from his horse, tried to strangle him with his bow before fleeing towards the Wude Hall, where Yuchi Jingde killed him. The princes' retainers dispersed when shown their heads.

According to the Jiu Tangshu and the Zizhi Tongjian, Gaozu was boating on a lake in the Palace City when Yuchi Jingde came, fully armed, to report the killings. At his advice the emperor ordered the remaining forces to submit, named Li Shimin heir within three days and abdicated about two months later, becoming a retired emperor. Father and son seem never to have been reconciled: in 632 Ma Zhou complained that Taizong rarely visited Gaozu, and the Daming Palace begun in 634 as his summer residence was unfinished when he died in 635.
xuanzang: Xuanzang was born Chen Hui, or Chen Yi, on 6 April 602 near present-day Luoyang in Henan, the youngest of four children of a family noted for its learning. After his father died in 611 he lived for five years with his elder brother, a monk, at the Jingtu Monastery in Luoyang, studying Mahayana and various early Buddhist schools. When the Sui dynasty collapsed in 618 the brothers fled to Chang'an and then to Chengdu in Sichuan, where they spent two or three years studying, including the Abhidharma-kośa Śāstra.

He later travelled through China looking for Buddhist books and reached Chang'an, then under Emperor Taizong of Tang. Like the earlier pilgrim Faxian, he was troubled by the incomplete and misinterpreted state of the scriptures that had reached China and by the competing theories in variant Chinese translations, and he sought original Sanskrit texts from India.

He defied his country's ban on travel abroad and made his way through Central Asian cities such as Khotan. In 630 he reached the kingdom of Agni, around Turpan, where a Buddhist king tried to persuade him to stay and equipped him with letters of introduction and funds when he declined. In India he studied at Nalanda with the monk Śīlabhadra. He left with Sanskrit texts carried by twenty packhorses and returned to China in 645. Emperor Taizong welcomed him but he refused the high civil appointments offered and retired to a monastery to translate.

With the emperor's support he set up a large translation bureau in Chang'an, drawing students from all over East Asia. He is credited with translating some 1,330 fascicles. His own strongest interest was Yogācāra, or Consciousness-only, which led to the Faxiang school, and his students Kuiji and Wŏnch'ŭk became influential authors.

In 646, at the emperor's request, Xuanzang completed the Records of the Western Regions. It is the longest and most detailed account of Central and South Asia by a Chinese Buddhist pilgrim and has helped to reconstruct the archaeological history of Bengal. It mixes first-hand report with hearsay and the implausible. His version of the Heart Sutra is the basis of Chinese commentaries and recitations across China, Korea, Vietnam and Japan. He died on 5 February 664 at Yuhua Palace in present-day Tongchuan, Shaanxi. His journey and its legends inspired the Ming novel Journey to the West by Wu Cheng'en, written about nine centuries after his death.
xue-ju: Xue Ju's clan came from Hedong Commandery, but his father Xue Wang moved the family to Jincheng. Said to be brave and strong, Xue Ju used his family's wealth to build ties with others, became an influential member of the local gentry and commanded the local militia. In 617, amid agrarian rebellions in eastern Gansu, the county magistrate Hao Yuan raised several thousand men and gave them to Xue Ju to command. In summer 617, at the feast held to send them off, Xue Ju, his eldest son Xue Rengao and 13 others seized Hao and declared a rebellion against the Sui.

Xue Ju arrested the local officials, opened the food stores to the poor and took the title Hegemonic Prince of Western Qin, perhaps echoing Xiang Yu's title. Joined by local rebels such as Zong Luohou, he soon held much of eastern Gansu, and in autumn 617 he declared himself Emperor of Qin, making his wife Lady Ju empress and Xue Rengao crown prince, and moved his capital to Tianshui. Traditional accounts describe him as cruel, killing captured soldiers or cutting off their tongues and noses, and say this cost him the following he hoped for.

Early in 618 Xue Rengao was badly defeated by Li Shimin, son of Li Yuan, the Sui general who held Chang'an. Xue Ju asked his officials whether emperors had ever surrendered, but Hao Yuan talked him out of it and became his chief strategist. Xue Ju then defeated the generals Jiang Mo, Dou Gui and Liu Shirang and sought an alliance with the Eastern Tujue and Liang Shidu to take Chang'an, but the Tujue general Ashina Duobi backed out.

In summer 618 Xue Ju attacked Jing Prefecture of the new Tang dynasty. Li Shimin, sent to resist him, built up his defences and tried to wear him out, but Xue Ju ambushed the Tang forces at Qianshui Plain, inflicting casualties of 50 to 60 per cent, and Li Shimin withdrew to Chang'an. Hao urged an immediate march on Chang'an, but Xue Ju fell ill and died. Xue Rengao succeeded him and gave him the posthumous name Wu, but was defeated by and surrendered to Li Shimin three months later, before he could properly bury his father.
xue-rengao: Xue Rengao, also known as Xue Renguo, was the eldest son of Xue Ju, a militia commander at Jincheng, in modern Lanzhou. In the summer of 617 father and son, with 13 others, seized the county magistrate Hao Yuan at a feast and proclaimed a rebellion against the Sui dynasty. Xue Ju made his son Duke and soon Prince of Qi, and with the general Zong Luohou the young man brought nearby commanderies under his father's rule. When Xue Ju claimed the title of Emperor of Qin that autumn, Rengao became crown prince, and his capture of Tianshui made it the capital.

He was said to be strong, a fine rider and archer whom his army thought a match for 10,000 men, but greedy and cruel. Accounts tell that he roasted Yu Li, son of the Sui official Yu Xin, over a fire and had his flesh cut off for his soldiers to eat. His father warned that such cruelty would destroy the state and the clan. Around the new year of 618 he suffered a major defeat at the hands of Li Shimin.

Xue Ju fell ill and died in the autumn of 618, after defeating Li Shimin and as he prepared to attack Chang'an, and Xue Rengao succeeded him as emperor. He fended off the Tang general Dou Gui, crushed the forces of Li Shuliang, Prince of Changping, by means of a feigned surrender and an ambush, and captured Chang Da. But many of his father's generals, with whom he had been on poor terms, feared him and gave him little support, and Hao Yuan, his father's chief strategist, grieved himself into illness and died.

Three months after his accession Li Shimin returned, defeated Zong Luohou at Qianshuiyuan and attacked Xue Rengao, who withdrew into the city of Gaozhi. His soldiers began surrendering to the Tang in large numbers, and he was forced to surrender himself. Li Shimin took his brothers and Zong Luohou into his army as officers, but Xue Rengao was taken to Chang'an and executed on the orders of Emperor Gaozu of Tang, together with his generals Wu Shizheng and Zhang Gui.
xue-rengui: Xue Rengui, whose formal name was Xue Li, was born in 614 under Emperor Yang of Sui. Little of his early life was recorded except that he was said to be a poor farmer and that his wife was surnamed Liu. In 644, as Emperor Taizong of Tang prepared to attack Goguryeo, Lady Liu urged him to seek honours in the army before reburying his ancestors, and he volunteered under the general Zhang Shigui.

At the front he rescued the general Liu Jun'ang from encircling Goguryeo troops, killed their commander and hung his head on his saddle, which won him promotion. Before the city of Ansi in 645 he charged the relief army of Ko Yŏnsu and Ko Hyejin in white armour with a ji and two bows. The Goguryeo army broke, and Taizong, who had asked who the man in white was, rewarded him with gold, silk and a command in the imperial guards.

Under Emperor Gaozong he climbed the gate of Wannian Palace during a flash flood in 654 to warn the emperor, who escaped as the water reached his bedchamber. In 657 he advised releasing the captive family of the Nishu chief, who then joined the Tang against Ashina Helu, and in 659 he defeated the Goguryeo general Wen Shamen and captured the Qidan chief Abugu, for which he was made Baron of Hedong.

Against the Tiele coalition in 661 he killed three champions with three arrows, but after their surrender had the ten and several thousand others killed; he was arrested for this and released when Gaozong judged his achievements greater than his crimes. In 668 he took Buyeo and some 40 cities before joining Li Ji at Pyongyang. After Goguryeo fell he was made protector general there and Duke of Pingyang, and was said to have won the allegiance of its people for a while.

After the defeat of 670 he was arrested, released and stripped of his posts, and probably in 675 he was exiled to Xiang Prefecture for reasons the records do not make clear. Recalled in 681, he died in March 683, and his sons Xue Ne and Xue Chuyu also served as generals. His life was dramatised in the Yuan play Xue Rengui's Glorious Return Home by Zhang Guobin and the Qing novel Xue Rengui's Campaign to the East; folklore makes him father of the fictional general Xue Dingshan, and he appears as a door god in Chinese and Taoist temples and as a general god in Korean shamanism.
xuzhou: Xuzhou, also known as Pengcheng, is a prefecture-level city in north-western Jiangsu province. It lies at the junction of four provinces, Jiangsu, Shandong, Henan and Anhui, in a natural gap between the Shandong Hills and the North China Plain. It stands at the south-eastern end of the North China Plain, on deep alluvial deposits from the migrations of the Yellow River, and limestone hills rise abruptly from the floodplain, the highest of them Dadong Mountain at 361 metres. The city is the ancestral home of the Han dynasty imperial family and is rich in Han archaeological remains.

Archaeological remains in the region are largely associated with the Dawenkou culture. In the Shang dynasty a polity called Dapeng, or Peng, associated with the Dongyi, dominated the area, and it was subordinated to Shang authority after the campaigns of King Wu Ding. After Qin unification the region was organised as a commandery. During the collapse of Qin, Pengcheng became a centre of Chu revival: Emperor Yi of Chu moved his seat there in 208 BCE, and in 206 BCE Xiang Yu made it the capital of Western Chu. Despite his victory at the Battle of Pengcheng in 205 BCE the city passed to Han control, and in 202 BCE it became the capital of the Chu Princedom under Liu Jiao.

In 154 BCE Prince Liu Wu joined the Rebellion of the Seven Princes. After his defeat his Shizishan tomb nevertheless exceeded the usual limits and contained gold-threaded jade burial suits. After the Revolution of 1911 the railways completed in 1912 and 1915 made Xuzhou a junction and a recurring target for rival factions. General Zhang Xun used it as a base and held four Xuzhou Conferences in 1916 and 1917.

Xuzhou had about 9.08 million inhabitants at the 2020 census. Its modern coal industry began with the Jiawang Coal Mine in 1882, and for decades that was the only industrial-scale coal extraction in Jiangsu. Most local mines have since closed, and the city has become a centre of heavy machinery manufacturing. It is a major rail hub where the Beijing-Shanghai line meets the east-west Land Bridge corridor.
